speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had to seek the same sources of information as my hon. friend, and I have been unable to get a specific answer to the last question he put for the reason that heretofore, as my hon. friend knows, there has been no marketing of halibut livers. I believe that there is a considerable amount of cod liver oil manufactured from halibut liver, and I am interested in knowing if that process is going on in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Such as has been used hitherto has been imported entirely from the United States. My information is that the use of halibut liver oil is in addition to the demand which hitherto existed for cod liver oil exclusively and that the use of halibut liver oil is increasing quite rapidly.

I understand that representations came from British Columbia for this change in the tariff due to the fact that American halibut livers were being landed at Prince Rupert and were having to pay a duty. I understand the suggestion was made that they could be manufactured in Canada if they were allowed to be admitted duty free. Can my hon. friend tell me whether or not the product will be marketed in Canada or used for export to the United States and other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not quite right in saying that they have been landed in Canada. As a matter of fact the duty prohibited their being landed. They were shipped by vessel back to the United States

or were dumped overboard. I believe the idea behind the request that they should be admitted free of duty is that we might have another industry in Canada developed. The demand in Canada, as I understand it, is comparatively limited and for a time at all events they will have to seek the export market for the major portion of the halibut liver oil produced. My information comes from the trade and is not based on any actual statistics or on a very wide degree of experience. But such is the expectation of the industry.

My point is that in view of the fashion nowadays, with which I do not agree, to find out whether or not there is a possibility of supplying the home market entirely with homemade products rather than to export products, it seems to me that before changes are made in tariff items affecting natural products we should know whether the natural products which we produce in this country are sufficient to supply the demand for the finished product which is made from them. As I understand it the minister has not been able to get that information and I have been unable to get it, and I find a difficulty in intelligently discussing or voting on the item which proposes a change and proposes to admit free natural products from foreign countries which may come into competition with our own products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend get
the statement on jute? If he did, they were pinned together.

I do not seem to have
the one on jute twine either. The point about the matter is that this item was one in respect to which the Minister of National Revenue had attempted under section 43 of the customs act to fix an arbitrary value for duty purposes. It was one of the items as to which 
it was alleged that the minister had lost the power of fixing an arbitrary value for duty purposes by reason of the amendment of November, 1932. Notwithstanding the fact that the section was repealed in November, 1932, and another section substituted which provided for the exemption of British goods from the power of the minister to fix an arbitrary value for duty purposes, the customs appraiser went ahead and imposed an arbitrary value on hats and hoods. This was appealed to the tariff board. Some time this spring-I have not the date but I think some time before March-the tariff board made an order holding the minister had no power to fix an arbitrary value for duty purposes, in other words, holding that the section of the act of 1932 was effective and that British goods were not to be subject to arbitrary valuation, and ordered, as I understand the matter, that a refund be made to the importer. I want to ask the minister whether the refund was made to the importer following the judgment of the tariff board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is
confusing the reference to the supreme court which arose under part II with the present case which is a hearing under part I. Whether that be so or not, I will say to my hon. friend that I shall have to get the information from the Department of National Revenue. I have made no particular inquiry recently but so far as my knowledge goes there has been no refund. I have no definite information on the point and I shall have to get that from the Department of National Revenue.

I think my hon. friend is right. I want him to understand clearly that I am not in any way confusing proceedings under part 1 and under part 2. Under part 1 the tariff board has power to make investigation and state facts on which the ministry may make decisions as to whether or not tariff items shall be amended. Under part 2 the tariff board have a judicial power, the same power as the board of customs previously had, to make decisions and to give effect to them. My complaint is that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) and this government are perfectly willing to take the recommendations of the tariff board under part 1 when they increase tariffs but they absolutely disregard binding decisions of the tariff board under part 2 which do away with arbitrary valuations and in effect decrease tariffs. That is my point ini a nutshell. This is a good example of it. Here we have hats, hoods and shapes which are included in an item moved by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) the other day and pro-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
viding for a specific duty. A short time ago we had the tariff board making an order that hats, hoods and shapes should not be subject to arbitrary valuations for duty purposes. That order was completely disregarded by the government. As the minister says, there has been no refund made to the importers, notwithstanding that the tariff board under the powers given by statute ordered such refund. My hon. friend says: Well, there was a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada as to the powers of the tariff board. Let me point out that that reference is not in connection with hats, hoods and shapes, but in connection with jute twine, and that reference, as I have had occasion to point out before, only settles one question, namely: Had the tariff board power to decide that jute twine did not come under the provisions of the act of November, 1932? It has no reference whatever to what we are talking about to-day, hats, hoods and shapes. The government flouts the tariff board in disregarding the decisions which the tariff board have made under part 2, but seems to be only too happy to take the suggestions of the tariff board under part 1 and provide for increases of duty. I submit that was not our conception of the way the tariff board was to be treated when it was constituted under an act of this parliament. I protest in the strongest possible way against that manner of dealing with tariff matters. If we are going to have a tariff board let us endeavour to follow their rulings, not follow them when it results in increasing duties and forget all about them when they say that duty shall be refunded or that the customs appraiser shall cease to make arbitrary valuations for duty purposes.
While I am on my feet let me say that the customs appraiser in the jute twine case put on an arbitrary value for duty purposes which resulted in effect in an ad valorem duty of 82 per cent. That decision was upset by the tariff board, and when the board came to make a recommendation in regard to duty, instead of 82 per cent which the minister was intent on imposing, they only suggested a duty of 274 per cent. It shows how tariff mad my hon. friends and the Department of National Revenue1 have gone. I submit that if we are to have a tariff board we ought at least to attempt to follow its recommendations not only under part 1 but part 2 as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall not attempt to follow my hon. friend in a discussion of the circumstances surrounding the case submitted to the supreme court, arising out of circumstances which are well known to the committee. It will be time enough to do that after the supreme court has made its finding. I do not even raise the point that the matter is sub judice. But what I do want to point out is that while hon. gentleman opposite may differ from us as to whether their attitude with respect to the tariff is right and ours wrong, the government has in every instance accepted the findings of the tariff board on matters of fact. Without any exception, when they have made findings of fact we have brought recommendations to the house in strict conformity therewith. The reference to the supreme court has not to do with a question of fact; the difficulty arises out of a question of law, as to the jurisdiction and authority of the tariff board acting in the stead of the old board of customs appraisers. That is an entirely different matter. I think it is quite fitting and proper that that matter should be cleared up. But I submit with all deference to my hon. friend that is an entirely different matter from accepting as we have in every instance the findings of the tariff board on matters of fact.

May I say to my hon. friend that his statement shows that he has misconceived the situation entirely. The decision of the tariff board in the jute twine case was that the minister should not fix an arbitrary value for duty purposes, and a similar decision was made in the hats, hoods and shapes case while in the tinplate Case they decided that tinplate was not of a class or kind made in Canada. These decisions were on questions of fact and not of law. Those were so far matters of fact that in the jute twine case an appeal was asserted to the governor in council on the question of fact as to whether or not the arbitrary value on jute twine was the correct value for duty purposes. My hon. friend must not draw that red herring across the trail. The reference to the supreme court was an attempt by the governor in council to get away from the decision on the question of fact by claiming that the tariff board had not the authority to make the order which they did in connection with the jute twine case. But the fact remains that the decisions of the tariff board in all three cases were on questions of fact, namely, what duty should be charged and what was the valuation upon which the rate of duty should be assessed. Those decisions stand unchallenged, because this government, although there was an appeal to them in connection with the jute twine case, have not seen fit even at this late date to decide it.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
What do they do? They refer to the supreme court the question whether the tariff board had authority. If they thought they had jurisdiction why did they not meet and decide the question of fact whether the jute twine ought to be valued at a value fixed by the minister and the duty assessed accordingly? What they said was: We will not decide the merits at all, whether A who imported these goods paid too much duty, but we will draw a red herring across the trail, skate around it and submit to the supreme court the question whether the tariff board have jurisdiction. After all the essential question in connection with commerce is, how much duty shall be paid. That is the essential thing from the point of view of the importer, the producer and the consumer, not whether the tariff board has jurisdiction but how much duty shall be paid. This government had the opportunity to decide that question or not to decide it, and they took the course of not deciding it. They referred to the Supreme Court of Canada the question of the jurisdiction of the tariff board, leaving untouched the decision of the board that as a matter of fact the value of jute twine for duty purposes was as it should have been after the act of November, 1932, had been repealed. I say that my hon. friend is wrong when he suggests that this government has followed the tariff board on questions of fact. This government have disregarded the decisions of the tariff board on questions of facts, and rather than face those decisions they have made reference to the Supreme Court of Canada as to the jurisdiction of the board on questions of law. I say that my point stands as I made it unchallenged; under part 1 they have accepted the recommendations of the tariff board as to increases of duty, but under part 2 they have studiously avoided following the recommendations and decisions of the tariff board that duty should be remitted and arbitrary valuations not imposed. Again I say that is not what was intended when the tariff board machinery was set up in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not those figures before me. Of course, my hon. friend is familiar with the general purpose we had in mind. We were confronted with this situation: The old item 1049 was brought into existence in 1925 for very good reason, namely, that coke came into Canada duty free, whereas if you wanted to manufacture coke in Canada the manufacturer was penalized by having to pay a duty of 50 cents a ton. As the tariff then stood it was designed to make it to the advantage of the manufacturer to manufacture the commodity which he used. What was done was that item 1049 was introduced to the tariff, giving a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty on coal converted into coke in by-product coke ovens. All that did was to place the manufacturer of coke in Canada on a parity, less one per cent, with the manufacturer in the United States, and it was done for the reasons I have indicated. But in the yeaT 1931 we placed one dollar a ton duty on coke, and removed entirely the reasons which occasioned item 1049 being applied in the first instance. Then there arose the situation that the manufacturer of coke in a gas plant who was selling coke in a given market found himself in competition with coke being manufactured by a by-product coke oven. The gas plant man was paying 75 cents duty on his coal, and the man with the by-product coke oven was not paying anything. That was the situation with which we were confronted. Either we had to widen the item or we had to cut it out. What we did was to split the difference. One reason for this amendment was the thought that it would inflict less hardship upon those who had hitherto enjoyed the drawback and would confer a very marked advantage upon a large number of users who could now enjoy the drawback of one-half the amount. While undoubtedly it will result in hardship to one or two important importers who have hitherto enjoyed the larger drawback, having regard to the country as a whole, we believe the result will be beneficial and it certainly will be more equitable.

I
do think that the by-product coke ovens to which the drawback was extended on account of their manufacture of metallurgical as well as domestic coke-

did not accomplish at Hamilton, and the other was to have a competitor for anthracite coal which would have a controlling influence upon the price of that commodity to the consumer. speechtext: For a number of years my hon. friend was Minister of Mines and he has had very intimate contact with the industry. I do not think he oan sustain that argument. Our feeling has been that that was a blow rather than an assistance to the Nova Scotia coal industry. I am not trying to raise this for the purpose of creating any party atmosphere with respect to this matter and I hope my hon. friend will accept my assurance upon the point. I cannot see how this proposal will affect the Nova Scotia coal industry prejudicially. I may say to him that our object in adopting this method was entirely different. We felt that an injustice had been created as between different producers in Canada of the same commodity.
It is not the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend Bays that it is not the same commodity. For the sake of argument let us assume that the quality of coke produced in a by-product coke oven is superior to that produced in a gas retort plant. The fact of the matter is that they are both coke, they are both fuel and they sell in the same manner. It cannot be to the disadvantage of the manufacturer of the superior product to be placed in even competition with the man who is producing an inferior product. So far as the manufacturer of t'he quality commodity is concerned, it seems to me that he is not prejudiced to the slightest degree. I admit that the situation in Montreal is a real one as it presents problems which are not common to any other industry affected by this drawback item. That matter gave me a great deal of concern. In the first place, the dollar per ton duty on coke was of relatively small advantage as they were faced with the free entry of British coke. That was the difficulty in the case of Montreal but it does not apply to the other coke ovens situated inland. Coke is a very bulky commodity and they are not subject to the same degree of competition under the British preferential tariff. If we find that any better method can be devised or put through after practical experience, we shall do so. Should any injustice appear in individual cases, for example, with respect to the Montreal coke manufacturing company, we will have to deal with the situation another year.
I do not think the change will in any way increase the consumption of Canadian coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I know my hon. friend to my left (Mr. Ralston) did not agree with me and he has strenuously fought the idea from its inception believing that Canadian coal was entitled to protection, but I am not quarrelling with him about that. I think the minister should put on record the difference in principle between what is now proposed and what he proposed in bis budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wording as we now have it provides the equivalent of what was introduced in the budget as a ten per cent tax on gold production. In other words a tax of twenty-five per cent on the exchange premium is the equivalent as nearly as may be of a ten per cent tax on production, with this distinction, that these provisions ensure that the tax will only come from those mines which have been regular dividend payers. For example if a mine paid a dividend in the year 1932, and did not pay a dividend in 1933, it would not be subject to this tax. Only those companies which paid dividends during the years 1932 and 1933 and for the six months' period ending March 31, 1934, will be subject to the tax. The wording, "gold deposited for sale at the Royal Canadian Mint produced from ore mined in Canada by producers of gold" excludes from the operation of the tax placer gold and scrap gold. There is one other feature; that is that the companies which pay the tax will be able to secure credit on this tax to the extent that they pay income tax. Those are the only changes from the original proposal.

I congratulate my hon. friend on the change he has made. While he says these are the "only" changes, I think they are most vital to the gold mining industry of the country. When I had occasion to address the house after my ho>n. friend had delivered his budget speech I stressed the point that what my hon. friend should not do was to tax production, but that if a tax must be imposed on the gold-mining industry of the country it should be imposed on profits. Secondly, I stressed the fact that he should not tax mines which were in the development stage. There are plenty of mines which are producing some gold but production and profits from these have in the very nature of things to be plowed back in order that the mine may reach a stable and satisfactory producing position. My hon. friend has met the first point by providing that the tax shall be on the premium and not, as in the original proposal, on t'he price itself; and by providing further that the tax shall only be paid by mines which have paid dividends, thus taking care of the point that only those mines which have profits shall pay it. In the same way he has met t'he point that mines which are only in the development stage shall not be taxed, because these mines have not yet started to pay dividends. I think the tax is much more equitable in this form. It is a radical change from what was proposed in the budget. Far be it from me to suggest that my hon. friend has taken any suggestion
Special War Revenue Act

or hint from this side of t'he house but still I am glad to note that his proposals meet the points which were made at the time his budget was criticized. May I say that the third point, namely that the tax paid is to be credited on account of income tax, shows how thoroughly and absolutely 'he has adopted the principle I endeavoured to lay down that only paying mines and only profits shall be taxed for the purpose of raising revenue from this particular industry.

I want to say
a word in regard to this tax on gold, particularly with reference to the exemption of placer gold, as provided under the amendment. It will be remembered that when the tax was imposed in the first place it was a tax on the total production of gold, placer as well as lode. That had a very unfortunate bearing on the production of placer gold in my own district. As one who probably comes in closer contact with that class of goldmining than any other person in the house I would like to explain the effect that a ten per cent tax on placer gold production would have in my district. Since the depression hit Canada we have in the neighbourhood of a thousand men in the Cariboo district producing placer gold individually by rocking on the bars and benches there. Now these men are of a class who are doing their utmost to keep off relief.	They resorted to this
method of earning a living and undertook this laborious work-because it is hard, difficult work and the returns are very small-and I thought it was rather an imposition on men of that kind to take ten per cent of their total production when they were doing their best to relieve the country of their maintenance. I cannot say exactly what the returns obtained by these men are, but from my own knowledge gained through purchasing the gold from them I would say that during the year 1932 when this operation started practically, I bought something like .810,000 or $12,000 worth of gold and kept pretty accurate track of the amount of work put into the production of that gold. As nearly as I could figure the wages that these men were making from this operation were between 50 and 60 cents a day. Now you can understand that with a thousand men in my district working for such wages through their anxiety to keep off relief, the proposal of the government to take a ten per cent rake off from their production was not very popular. I appreciate very much, as do the placer miners of the Cariboo district, the fact that they have been relieved of that taxation.
fMr. Ralston.]
In order to show how much it affects the production of gold, last year the total production in Canada with premium added was something like $85,000,000. The production of placer gold is practically confined to the Yukon and British Columbia. The production of placer gold in British Columbia last year was $357,000 and in the Yukon about $1,000,000. Remember that the Yukon production at the present time is taxed by the federal government. I think it is two and a half per cent at the present time, but at one time the federal government levied a tax on twenty per cent on the total production of the Yukon.
I should like to give just a few figures in regard to mining in British Columbia. In 1933 there were 155 new mining companies incorporated in that province, of which 145 were gold mining companies. Most of these concerns, of course, are lode mining companies. Last year the British Columbia government issued 16,000 free miners' licences, the greatest number of such licences ever issued in that province in any one year. That is accounted for by the fact to which I just referred, that so many unemployed men resorted to the bars and benches of the different rivers of that province in order to recover as much of the gold from the gravel as they possibly could. I may say that some of those men who were well versed in the science of prospecting, who knew just where to go and how to save the fine gold, made very handsome profits. The majority of these men, being inexperienced and not knowing how to prospect, where to look for the gold or how to save it after they found it, made very small returns. In addition to those free miners' licences the British Columbia government also issued provisional free miners' certificates entirely without charge, which carried the privilege, for these men who were trying to make their living, of having their claims recorded free and working their claims without charge. So it will be seen by the committee that the government of British Columbia has been working in cooperation with these men in order to give them an opportunity to make a living in that way.
There is just one other point I should like to mention in connection with the expansion of gold mining in British Columbia. The territory which is producing the greater part of this gold is the territory served by the Pacific Great Eastern railway, and the tonnage hauled over that railway last year was greatly increased through the extension and expansion of the gold mining industry. That road

Special War Revenue Act
hauled 6,472 tons of freight in 1933 as compared with 2,137 tons in 1932, which gives an idea of what the gold mining industry does for the railway serving the territory in which the expansion is taking place.
Let me once more express my appreciation for the modification that has been made in the original proposal, and at the same time I should like to express to the Minister of Finance and the government the appreciation of those who are engaged in that industry in British Columbia.

I, too, should like to congratulate the minister on his amendment. As the provision was introduced it would have put a great many of the smaller gold mines out of business; there is no doubt of that. Undoubtedly it would have hampered the mines giving the greatest amount of employment as well, so I think the minister should be congratulated on having made the change. Undoubtedly the profit tax is the fairest tax that can be imposed, though in my mind I have a doubt as to whether this is a proper field for the federal government to enter. It seems to me that if a tax on gold was to be imposed it should have been imposed by the provinces, because there are only about three of the provinces that are gold producing. However, I am not going to quarrel with the minister on that aspect of the matter; I know how badly he needs revenue, and I am informed that he will get about as much by this method as was anticipated in the proposal first made. I do think this will have a stabilizing effect on the production of mines which have had some difficulty in carrying on and which, as I have pointed out, of necessity must give a greater amount of employment than the mines which now will be affected. I am not so sure about the retroactive aspect of the amendment. Is that not a new departure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; there is nothing
retroactive in it.
I understood that it was retroactive to 1933.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, that has reference only to companies which paid dividends in that year; it is not a tax on the gold produced. Companies had to pay dividends in 1932, 1933 and the six months prior to March of this year; otherwise they were not taxed at all. That is merely used for the purpose of defining those companies that should pay the tax as and from the 19th day of April. That is all.
I could discuss this matter at length; it is rather an interesting subject, but I will deal with only one point. May I say to my hon. friend from Edmonton that the taxation of the mining industry is one thing that quite properly might be a field of taxation reserved to the provinces, but the tax on the premium on gold is an entirely different thing. The price of gold is fixed under the Currency Act as a matter of statute; its value is determined by the legislation of this parliament, and with all deference I submit that the tax on the premium is peculiarly within the right of this parliament and does not interfere in any way with the right of the provinces to tax the mining industry as such. Their taxation in that respect can be levied if they see fit to do so.
They can do so now; there is nothing to prevent them from taxing the mining industry, as they probably will in due course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is so.

The hon. member for
Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) stated that in the last few years he had purchased a great deal of gold from miners. Paragraph 10 of this section makes it unlawful for anyone but the producer to ship gold to the mint. From this section I take it that the original producer must transfer his gold to the mint, and that it cannot be purchased by anyone other than the mint. I should like to know from the minister if that assumption is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be permitted to say a word in that connection. Placer mining is in a peculiar position. If the provision that producers must bring their gold to the mint were strictly adhered to it would debar hundreds and thousands of individual placer miners who gather up small quantities of placer gold in the Yukon and in British Columbia. So it is a real convenience to them to give them an opportunity of disposing of their gold on the spot and receiving cash from some individual who is prepared to buy it from them. That individual may gather together a considerable volume of such gold and, in turn, send it to the mint. My hon. friend will observe that the minister may issue a permit which would cover just that case in point. It is an entirely different thing from the gold which comes from a producer such as a company which produces several hundred ounces of gold in a year, as compared with the individual placer miner who produces perhaps only a few ounces.
Special War Revenue Act

For the information of those of us who are on the outside and do not know the inside story of gold mining, would the minister tell us how the master of the mint knows placer gold from gold mined in other ways?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed it is very easily distinguishable. The gold coming from each mine, as a matter of fact, has distinguishing qualities to an extent that the moment the master of the mint sees a brick he can tell, with a great degree of accuracy, from which mine it has come. There are different colours, qualities and bloom, as the hon. member for Pictou has reminded me. Furthermore, in every case certificates of origin are required.

I wish to thank the minister for his explanation and, with other hon. members, to congratulate him upon the amendments. We must not forget. that the mining of gold is made possible by the investing public, and in connection with the imposition of a tax of this kind they must be considered. Not only t'he operators of gold mines and miners of placer gold are interested, but there are people from coast to coast who have put their money into mining ventures and made it possible for these operators and miners to carry on. Therefore, if the change made by the minister brings about a more equitable arrangement, I should like to congratulate him. I do not say he took his cue from the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth, but I do say there was a general appeal from people throughout the country that changes should be made, and I think the Minister of Finance was wise in making the change.

Old teeth, for instance,- bridges, and that sort of thing, melted down.

They must be handed in in their original form?

So that if old gold comes in bars, melted down, it will not be purchased by the mint?

The minister does not propose to put teeth in this law, then?

There is no contemplated change in the existing legislation?

I should like once more to revert to this matter of the price of old gold.
I have in mind an instance where a person came from the United States bringing a quantity of old gold in bars. It was declared illegal to bring it in, because a declaration

Special War Revenue Act
was not made at the border. That was the only illegality committed. After he had straightened out his difficulties with the department at Washington this [DOT] person retained parties in Canada for the purpose of selling the gold. He thought he would be able to do so, gaining the advantage of the premium, but he was unable to negotiate a sale because of the fact that the gold was not produced from Canadian mines. The question of the odd five dollar gold piece ought not to have been considered, because if there were any they would be American, and not Canadian. In that respect, therefore, he did not break the law. Why was it he was not given the regulation amount of $35 an ounce for his gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the reasons I indicated a moment ago, our regulations state that gold shall be submitted to the mint in its original form. This is done for the express purpose of preventing old gold being melted down, and gold coin being added to it.
Canadian gold coin?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, or British sovereigns,
or the five dollar gold pieces of the United States, none of which, as coins, are worth more than their face value.

Why should we declare a
protectorate over American gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because the United States coins are legal tender in Canada. We wish to protect only the legitimate trade, and not that trade which arises out of the opportunity to make an easy dollar.

The house resumed from Friday, June 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 91, respecting shipping-Mr. Duranleau-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
On section 2-Definitions.

Mr. Chairman, before we proceed further with this bill I should like to know what the government has decided since last Friday evening. I was not here when discussion on the bill started. As everybody can see, this is a very bulky billi It is true that it has been considered by the Senate this year and that it has also been before a Senate committee which has gone over it very carefully, as it did also last year, but if it took the Senate all of last session and practically all of this session to be able to appreciate the contents of this bill, I think it is only fair to the members of the House of Commons that the same opportunity should be given to them. But here we are in the dying hours of the session, on the very last lap, and this bill is presented for our consideration. I do not think it is fair to ask the members of the House of Commons at this stage of the session to examine this bill carefully, clause by clause-the clauses are very numerous-and to examine all the rules and regulations and all the schedules that are attached to the bill.
But there is another reason. Although this bill was considered by the Senate last year I have been told that the Senate received many delegations from the pilotage authorities of the various districts throughout the country both this year and last. There are members of the House of Commons who would like to _ have some knowledge of the discussions that took place over there. Of course we cannot be expected to follow the discussions that take place in the committees of the Senate on the various bills that are later submitted for our consideration, for as hon. members will recall, this year we have had to consider in this house most important legislation, the revision of the Bank Act, which we passed only recently; the companies act, the act creating the new central bank, and many other pieces of legislation of the highest importance.
My attention has also been drawn to the fact that there are in this bill certain rules and regulations which affect the fishermen of the lower part of the province of Quebec and of the maritime provinces, and I am informed that the owners of schooners and other vessels and boats will have to pass examinations and obtain certain classified
Canada Shipping Act

certificates in order to operate their boats. In our part of the country and in the maritime provinces I am told that a great many of these people will be put at a great disadvantage if this bill is passed, because while most of them have been brought up to the sea a good many of them I daresay on account of their age and physical condition, the condition of their eyesight and other things, may not be able to pass the examination prescribed. If they cannot, they will be put to great expense in engaging the services of a certificated man to put in charge of the ship and the crew.
There are also in the bill certain clauses and rules and regulations which affect the pilotage district of Montreal and pilots of vessels coming from the maritime provinces and up the lakes, and especially affecting the pilots below Quebec. I am told on good authority by the assistant deputy minister, who is a very amiable and also a very responsible and competent authority in these matters, that these rules and regulations will not affect the certificates of pilots who have held their certificates for a good many years, but that they will affect the certificates of pilots in the future. This is a most important matter, and the situation of those pilots should be made clear when the bill is being discussed. I have received numerous communications, requests and petitions from the pilots of the district of Quebec concerning this very matter.
These are some features which right there stare us in the face. I am also mindful that as we proceed with the discussion of this bill other points which will come up for debate may take a considerable time. Last year when a similar bill was under consideration it was not proceeded with because of the serious -contentions made in relation to it, but the government saw fit to have a measure passed to protect sailors and others employed in vessels, the pilots being supposed to be protected also. On that occasion the Minister of Marine told us that it was of paramount importance that this measure be put through in order to protect those sailors and others. Now I am told that this bill that was passed last year by the House of Commons and assented to by the Senate did not come into effect. The government was in a great hurry to have the bill passed to protect those people but it did not see fit to pass an order in council to promulgate the bill and put it into effect. Apparently, however, nobody has suffered from the measure not being put into force. The same thing will happen to the present measure, and it might just as well

await its birth, origin and light of day for another year. For these reasons it might be laid over this year, as it is now nearly the end of the session. The shipping interests of the country will not suffer any harm if the passage of the bill is delayed for another year, and next session when we reconvene we shall have an opportunity to consider it and be able as members of the House of Commons and as truly representative of the people to give due and full consideration to the legislation. After five months of strenuous work as we have had it is not fair in the last days of this session to ask members to consider all the clauses of this bill and to give it the attention we would like to give, the same as we have given to other measures that have been laid before us in the last few weeks.
It is not sufficient to say that the Senate has considered the bill and reported favourably. I think it was the Minister of Justice who said the other day in connection with a bill concerning lotteries and sweepstakes that; the fact that it came from the Senate was not a certain certificate, and the house did not see fit to accept the proposals contained in that measure. It is all very well to say that the Senate is the superior body over all the people in this country, but when an important matter such as shipping comes up, the House of Commons should have the right and full opportunity of discussing every clause, subclause, schedule and anything else connected with the bill so as to be able to vote on it in an intelligent manner. Consideration by the Senate is all very well in certain cases, but we should not always take it for granted that we should pass any legislation just because it comes before us with their certificate.
Last year the question of the constitutionality of this legislation arose. I was not present when the minister spoke the other day, but this bill raises many serious questions with reference to the constitutionality of the law, and I should like to have more cogent and important reasons that we should be asked to put the stamp of our approval on this bill holus-bolus as apparently the government wants us to do, I for one protest against this measure being brought before us in the last days of the session. I remember a few years ago because bills were sent by the former government to the upper chamber in the dying days of the session, the Senate refused to consider them although they had been fully considered and passed by the House of Commons.
I for one would ask the government to reconsider its decision and see whether it would

Canada Shipping Act
not be well to put over this bill for another year. The government would be well advised if it would have the committee report progress and not have us asked to consider this bill again this year.

Am I right
in saying that the Senate has studied this measure in the past two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think hon. members have followed the consideration of this bill in the Senate. As I explained when it was introduced and when I spoke on the second reading, last year a similar bill was introduced in the Senate and studied by the standing committee on banking and commerce of that chamber. When the interested parties were before that committee the point was raised as to the power of the Canadian parliament to impose certain duties on British consuls or other officials in other countries when we had perhaps no such authority. So the bill was deferred to this session and we had to arrange with the British authorities in the meantime to settle the point. That was the only question raised last year. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain) spoke of the constitutionality of the legislation. I do not think there is now any ground for any fear, all these points have been settled.
How were they settled?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The bill before the
Senate last year had to be withdrawn. Practically the same bill with certain amendments was introduced this year, and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce of the Senate, where in turn a subcommittee was set up, where it was studied, I suppose, during two or three weeks. It was then referred back to the full committee on banking and commerce of the Senate, where again all interested parties were heard and slight amendments incorporated in the bill on the representations made. I would refer my hon. friend to the remarks I made on the second reading of the bill as they appear in Hansard of June 8 at page 3812.
The point raised by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay that the bill should stand over was raised by some of his colleagues last Friday. It was understood then that the government would consider the matter and after having done so and owing to public opinion, we feel we are bound to proceed with the bill. Though the debate took place late last Friday, I have been receiving since
then telegrams from interested parties urging the adoption of this measure. I can give my hon. friends the contents of telegrams we have so far received.
From what concerns?

speechtext:
I have received a
telegram from the National Association of Marine Engineers of Canada, Council No. 8 of Levis, recommending the immediate adoption of this bill. They say:
Shipping bill as passed by Senate a great improvement and greater protection to navigation in general.

speechtext: The Shipping Federation of Canada.

to a telegram of your own?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Not at all. These
wires have been received as a result of what they have read in the press since last Friday about the debate. The Canada Steamship Lines have also sent a long telegram urging adoption of this bill at this session. I heard my hon. friends last Friday; I heard also the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay and I would say that there are not more than ten or fifteen sections of the bill affected by their statement.

speechtext:
I am saying that from the debate last Friday it appears that there are not more than ten or fifteen sections on which there would be discussion or contest.
All the other sections of the bill are a reproduction of our present law.

Then they are in force
now.
Canada Shipping Act

speechtext:
They are in the
Canada Shipping Act or the load line convention or a reproduction of the safety at sea convention. All these conventions were ratified by this house two years ago and are the law of the land to-day.
My hon. friend says that only fifteen clauses are in dispute. I ask him if he understands from my remarks last Friday that that is the case.

speechtext:

hon. friend to state the sections of the bill that he intends to oppose.

bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Well, let us suppose
so; we must proceed. We can go on clause by clause and my hon. friends will do what they think is in the public interest.

The minister gave a list of

Since Friday.

It is funny.

speechtext: Have the fun you want. Let us proceed, and my hon. friends will have ample opportunity to discuss any sections of the bill.

My hon. friend has made the statement that the people of Canada are satisfied with this bill. I am asking him a definite question: Since this bill was passed by the Senate,-it was amended in a hundred different clauses by the Senate during two years and at the cost of a large amount of money
fMr. Casgrain.]

I want a definite answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend that not a single man from the east has opposed the bill that is before the house to-day.

Because they have not seen it. And that, Mr. Chairman, is my objection. What I want is to have this bill go to the shipping and business men all over Canada, whether on the Pacific coast or in Quebec or on the great lakes or the Atlantic provinces. I say this bill should not be forced through parliament, but these people should have a chance to study it. Here we have a bill of 497 pages which nobody has seen, which I say the minister himself has not read completely-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I beg your pardon.
Lord help you!

Well, perhaps the minister has read it; I must take his word for it. But I have spent a week since last Wednesday and so far have read only 74 pages out of the 497. The minister must have better knowledge than I because he has been to college and I have not, but I say that the people interested in this bill have never seen it and in the interests of the shipping and business people of this country, of the seamen and the fishermen and everyone else, I protest. It is not fair that the minister should ask that this bill be passed without due consideration.

Last Friday when this bill was before the house certain of us from the maritime provinces on both sides of the house made representations asking that for certain reasons which we considered important this bill should not be proceeded with. It was then suggested, I think by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), that in order to get the bill moving, one section or subsection should be adopted, and then the government would take time to consider whether they should proceed with the bill or on the request of representatives from the maritime provinces withdraw it till next session. Evidently the government has now decided to proceed. In order to justify that action t'he minister tells this committee that since last Friday he has received from various sources telegrams

Canada Shipping Act
asking that this bill be proceeded with immediately. I gather that he has received a telegram from the National Association of Marine Engineers of Canada, Levis section. Assume that it be from all the marine engineers of Canada, I do not care what section it comes from or the number, can the minister point out anything in this bill protecting the marine engineers that was not in the old act? He cannot do it. Therefore why should the marine engineers be in such a hurry to have this bill go through? The marine engineers' association of Canada looks after the interests of marine engineers, but we find in this bill section upon section that affects one of the largest industries in Canada, the fishing industry. Has the minister any representations from the fishermen's associations in the maritime provinces asking him to put the bill through in its present form? He cannot produce one line. Let me go further, and I am very earnest in this because I see the danger of almost absolute ruin to certain branches of our fishing industry if this bill goes through.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why?
I will tell you in a moment. If it goes through in its present form it will impose conditions on the fishing industry of this country with which they cannot comply.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: What sections?

There are many sections. If we are forced to go on with this bill I will endeavour to have those sections amended, but what is the position of any representative of the fishing districts of the maritime provinces to-day, when we have not had an opportunity of consulting with our people, of laying this bill before them, of discussing the dangers they may see and their opinions as to the remedies .to be proposed? We are not in a position to consider the bill. If you force us to go on with this bill you force us to attempt to carry out what we believe is in the best interests of the fishing industry, but even with the knowledge we have of that industry we may do an injustice to our people. That is why I feci so strongly in the matter.
The other reason mentioned by the minister had to do with a telegram received from the Shipping Federation of Canada, who, the minister told the committee, represent all interests. They do not. The interests represented by that association from whom the minister received his information are principally the deep water interests, those
concerned with communication between Canada and foreign countries and those engaged on the lakes, which are international waters to some extent. They have no authority to represent or speak for the men engaged in the fishing industry in this country, and that is another reason why we do not desire to proceed with this bill. The minister also says the Senate has considered the bill and that all interests were represented before the Senate committee. He read a telegram something to this effect, "In view of the fact that all interests were represented before tha Senate this bill should go through." I say that telegram is a lie. It states that all interests were represented before the Senate, but neither the minister nor anyone else can show that one single interest connected with the fishing industry was represented before the committee of the Senate. Therefore why force us to go on with this bill this session when I am convinced that no interest will suffer if it is put off? I am firmly of the opinion, however, that if it is put through in its present form very large interests will be detrimentally affected, and the Lord only knows what the end may be.

Mr. Chairman, I was before the Senate committee for a number of days following this bill while the hearings were going on. I shall not attempt to enumerate the interests represented! there, but many interests were represented and many witnesses were heard. During the time I was there, which included the better part of a week, I thought the bill received very careful attention, especially from a large body of men from the eastern provinces.
Who were they?

The senators who come
from the east. To the onlooker they gave the impression that they were not only deeply interested in the work which has been going on there for some three years, I think, but that they were intimately acquainted with it. Furthermore I noticed that the great majority of the sections are non^controversial. A great many of them deal with treaties; a great many of them are lifted out of the old act, and a large portion of the time spent on these sections was devoted to their arrangement, deciding the sequence in which they should appear, rather than in dealing with the purport of any particular sections.
I thought the house might be interested to know the impression obtained by one who followed the proceedings of that committee very carefully. In the heated state of mind in which some hon. gentlemen seem to be

I do not know whether they would care to proceed with the consideration of the bill, but I think if they attempt that course they will find that the controversial sections are very few and a long way apart.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government proposes to proceed with this bill. It has been twice before the Senate, it has received more consideration than any bill that has come before parliament for a very long time. It has been given more attention in detail than any measure that has been in either house for a very long period. It is the result of much effort in which the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) participated in 1929 in London, in directing the general principles that should govern this legislation. The bill was drafted, considered by experts, redrafted and considered in committee.
Who were the experts, please?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They were the gentlemen responsible for its legal provisions. The representatives of the various interests concerned made their statement before the committee. If there are very controversial sections in the bill they can stand as we proceed, and if the amendments suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite are such as appear to be in the public interest we shall be very glad indeed to adopt them. I trust that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) will recall the observations made by his distinguished leader a few days ago with respect to the duties of a member of parliament. In the light of that statement I am sure he will find some difficulty in accommodating his views as expressed this afternoon to those of his honoured leader.
We desire to proceed with the bill for the reasons I have given. We believe it is in the public interest, which is the paramount interest. If individuals find it inconvenient to particular interests we will always consider the public interest and the particular private interest affected, but the public interest must prevail. With that principle in mind we will proceed with the discussion of the bill.

I did not intend to speak again, but since the (Prime Minister has lectured me on my duties as a member I feel that I should make some reply to his remarks. It is true my right hon. leader did refer to the duties a member owes not only to himself but to the country as a whole. I do not need either my right hon. leader or the right hon. leader of the government to teach me any lessons in that regard. I have been long enough in public life to know the duty I owe to my constituents and to the pu' r:i at large.

This afternoon I am not pleading for my constituents, but I am pleading on behalf of one of the largest industries in Canada. I am speaking for the fishing industry on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and I am backed by representatives from those districts of our dominion. That industry, to my mind, is paramount to any protection this law may afford in connection with deep sea sailing, or the protection of engineers and captains of deep sea vessels. Therefore my opposition to the bill is not parochial. I have in mind the duty which, as a member of the House of Commons, I owe to all sections of Canada. As the principle has been laid down that the lesser must give in, for the benefit of the larger, may I say that to-day I am pleading on behalf of the larger. I am pleading on behalf of the fishing industry of Canada, as compared with the lesser interests of engineers and captains of vessels running from one country to the other. Under this legislation they are fully protected, and they were fully protected under the old legislation. There is no amendment in the new bill which affords protection contrary to that which was given them under the British act, the measure under which we have been operating since 1867. But in the adoption of the present measure as it stands an injustice would be perpetrated against one of the greatest industries in Canada, and as a member of the House of Commons with a full knowledge of my duty to my country and to myself I am pleading on behalf of that great industry, and against the smaller interests connected with marine engineers and deep sea captains.

I regret that this very voluminous document which is of such great importance should be placed before the house at this time, and that at this late hour of the session we should be asked to study it. Hon. members know that we cannot stay here all summer. If, as the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mir. Hackett) has said, the other chamber studied the measure for three years, surely that is sufficient indication as to the importance of and the difficulties in connection with the measure. I agree entirely with the Prime Minister (Mr, Bennett) as to the advisability of a revision of the shipping act; it must be done. So far as the constitutional point raised by the hon. member for Char-levoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) is concerned, I must say that I am of the opinion his fears are not well founded. I think however it is not fair at this late hour of the session to ask hon. members of the House of Commons to consider the bill. It is the result

Canada Shipping Act
of much work, as the Prime Minister and Minister of Marine have said. Undoubtedly it is a good thing that public business should originate in the Senate, but the fact remains that the country is not used to that procedure, and as a result the proceedings of the Senate are not followed as closely or as attentively as those of the House of Commons. With the exception of those hon. members who have been peculiarly interested in the measure, the country as a whole has certainly not become familiar with it.
They have not had a chance.

On the whole I must agree with hon. members who have said it would be better to give the people of Canada an opportunity to become better acquainted with the bill before we undertake to proceed with it.
We are on section 2 of the bill, and I notice that in this section there are 113 subsections. Does the committee wish me to read every one of them?

Yes, if it is necessary, but I should like to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

For two or three

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the representations which have been made should be the subject matter of inquiry in this matter. The government assumes full responsibility for the introduction of this bill, which arises from the conferences of 1926 and 1929. This bill is the result of what took place in London in 1929 and is one of the legacies which we inherited. For three years we have been endeavouring to give effect to it, and this is now the fourth year.

I do not think it is ncessary
for the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to intervene in this matter. Why does he not go back to mid-Victorian days, to the day of George I or to some time a thousand years ago? I think I am quite in order in asking this question of the Minister of Marine, and I do not think the Prime Minister had any right to interject what he did a moment ago. I have asked the minister if he has received certain representations in connection with this bill and I would like to know what they are. I contend that the fishing and shipping interests of this country are opposed to this bill. They do not know what it is, because they have not seen it, and we are now being asked to pass it in the dying days of the session. It came over from the Senate only five days ago, and I think the people of this country should have an opportunity to study it and decide whether it is right or wrong.

Shall the subsection carry?

No, the minister cannot answer, that is the trouble; he does not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I told the committee that for the past two or three years representations have been made to my officials and to myself. Surely my hon. friend is not serious when he asks me to give him the particulars of the representations made. Different associations have made representations in connection with the sections in which they are interested, and as we proceed with the bill and reach the sections in connection with which representations were made, I will give my hon. friend what he asks for if I am in position to do so. But I do not think it is fair to put the question in that way when we are dealing with subsection 2 of section 2, which concerns definitions.

Certainly it is proper for the minister in charge of this bill to tell us what is the object of the bill and what result it is going to have. This is a bill of 497 pages; it has 719 sections, it has 113 definitions and there are 224 pages of schedules. Surely the minister does not expect us to pass this bill when it has been before us for only four or five days. It is all right for the Prime Minister to want to close up this parliament in a few days, and I appreciate that, but-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am perfectly indifferent to that.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am perfectly willing to stay all summer.

All right, if you cannot go to have a holiday, neither can I, and we will stay. The Prime Minister and I agree that we will stay here until September* But even if we do stay until September, it is not fair that a bill of 497 pages, drafted by a lawyer from Vancouver, an honourable member in another place, in whose name the bill appears but who does not know a codfish from a haddock or an alewife from a hake, should be passed so quickly. This bill was sent here a week ago, and surely the Prime Minister does not expect us to pass it in a few days. Let us be fair about this thing. This bill means a lot to every man, woman and child in the maritime provinces, on the great lakes and on the Pacific coast. Surely the Prime Minister does not expect us to pass this bill in the few minutes taken by the Senate to pass it. Does the Prime Minister want us to do that? Has the Prime Minister read this bill? No, of course he has not. No one else has read it. I have been studying it for a week but how far have I got? Seventy-four pages [The Chairman.]
out of 497. Has the Prime Minister read one page? Has the Minister of Justice read two pages? Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce read ten pages? Has the Minister of Railways read fifteen pages? No. And yet the Prime Minister comes in here to-night and wants us to pass this bill in bulk, without giving it any consideration. Don't consult the fishermen or the sailors on the Atlantic coast or the Pacific coast; don't consult the men on the great lakes; just let us put this bill through so that we can get clear of parliament in a few days. I say, Mr. Chairman, that that is not fair. It has taken the Senate two years to pass this-I will not call it an amalgamated bill-what is it? It is a posthumous bill. It was conceived in sin and born in iniquity, and the Prime Minister wants us now to pass it without the opportunity for consideration. Surely he does not really want to do that, for he does not know what it is all about; he has not read the bill. There are hundreds of clauses in this bill which nobody has seen. The Prime Minister has not read them, and because the Senate passed the bill in three minutes, as they did a week ago, the Prime Minister now wants us to put this bill through. It is true that the bill was considered by a committee of the Senate, but who gave this bill to the Senate? A lawyer from Vancouver and a lawyer from Ottawa. Here is a bill, Mr. Chairman, which deals with the lives and the property of every business man on the Atlantic coast, on the Pacific coast and on the St. Lawrence. Surely the Prime Minister does not want us to put it through in such a hurry. .
Let us be fair about this tiling. Nobody will suffer if this bill goes over until another session. Nobody will be hurt. The seamen, the masters and the mates and everybody else concerned are not complaining. The Minister of Marine cannot show me one telegram or letter from anybody interested in the business life of this country who wants this bill passed at this session. Why, then, should the Prime Minister or the Minister of Marine want us to pass this bill now? Let it stand over for another session so that the shipping men and the business men can look it over, instead of rushing it through in the dying days of this session.
The Prime Minister says that we can sit here till September. Of course we can, but I would not want the Prime Minister with all his troubles and worries to have to face parliament for another two months. I would give him Wednesday nights off.
Here is an important bill of 497 pages, a bill which affects the shipping people and the business men of this country, and yet the

Canada Shipping Act
Prime Minister says:	You must pass this bill
before parliament prorogues. I say, Mr. Chairman, that before we proceed to do that, the Minister of Marine must give us reasons why this bill is introduced at this stage of the session. Let him tell us what he knows about it. The Minister of Marine cannot give any good reason why this bill is introduced at this moment. I say that with a bill like this, which has not been before the shipping industry of this country, which has not been before the ship owners and before the business men who are interested in shipping, there is only one thing to do, and that is to ask that this committee rise, and say that this bill should not pass now.

I would respectfully draw the attention of the committee to paragraph 2 of rule 58, which reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
We are on subsection 2 of section 2 of this bill. It seems to me that the discussion has travelled very far afield, and I would ask hon. gentlemen to stick a little more closely to the section.

Mr. Chairman, when the bill
came up for discussion on Friday evening, the very first clause was allowed to stand without discussion on the understanding that we proceed to section 2 and that then the committee would rise. It was the understanding of the committee that when the bill again came up hon. members would be allowed very considerable latitude on this section. It was the Minister of Finance, I think, who suggested that the committee should rise after calling section 2.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have no objection.
I am in the hands of the committee.

When the bill was up for
second reading, Mr. Chairman, there was no discussion upon it because it was understood that we would have a general discussion in committee, not confining ourselves to any particular section of the bill. Otherwise there would have been a lengthy discussion on the second reading.

I would like to ask, so as to clarify the position, how many sections of this bill are reenactments of the Merchant Shipping Act, how many are reenactments of sections from the revised statutes of Canada, and how many are new sections. It seems to me that there are very few new sections, but I do agree that some of those are worthy of very careful consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: For the information of the committee, during the recess I counted the new dispositions in the bill and I find that there are exactly seventy new enactments, sections and parts of sections. There may be in all about thirty or thirty-five new sections. The whole bill is a reproduction of the Merchant Shipping Act of 1894, a reproduction of the Canada Shipping Act, and a reproduction of the conventions which have been the law of the land since 1931, when the load line convention and the international convention for safety of life at sea were approved by this parliament. There are from thirty to thirty-five new sections in all. That is why I said to my hon. friends on Friday evening that if they would take the trouble over the week-end to look over the bill they would find that there were not many controversial sections. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that as we proceed to study the different sections my hon. friends will very shortly come to the conclusion that there is not so much to discuss.

It is very nice of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine to say that I should have spent the week-end in trying to arrive at a conclusion with regard to this bill, but evidently he does not appreciate the seriousness of the situation. My hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asks what new clauses there are in the bill. Let me say to him that the trouble with this bill is that the Marine department are back in the mid-Victorian era. They do not realize what has happened in the last thirty years. This bill is a composite bill drafted by certain officials in the Marine department, with the assistance of somebody else-I do not know who it is -who does not appreciate present conditions. If my hon. friend from York-Sunbury, who asked a question, will listen to me, I say that this is a composite bill drafted by somebody, first by a lawyer from Vancouver who perhaps deserved the money that the government paid him-he spent a year on it-and then by another lawyer. And what did they give him? A bill which is absolutely opposed to the business interests of the people of this country, to the interests of the fishing industry and of the marine industry. This bill takes us back to 1896 and 1906. I do not think the Prime Minister should be asked to father this bill or to say that he knows something about it. He does not. He is a lawyer from Calgary and my hon. friend opposite is a lawyer from York-Sunbury. But surely my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and my hon. friend from Inverness Mr. Mac-
Canada Shipping Act

dougall) and others who go down to the sea in ships and do business on the great waters should be allowed to express their views, and I think our views should be taken into consideration by this government. I would be delighted, if this bill were right, that the house should pass it in bulk just as the Senate did in three minutes. But I say to my hon. friend from York-Sunbury that this bill, this illegitimate child of somebody, for that is what it is to those who have had a chance to study it, is not in the interests of the shipping industry or of the business men of this country. Has my hon. friend from Pictou had a chance to go over the 497 pages of this bill? Has my hon. friend from Inverness read the 719 clauses of this bill?
I have read all the sections of the bill and I want to say that I do not see any section that prejudices the interests of the fishermen.

I am delighted that my hon. friend is such a strong supporter of this government that he will say that, but I want to say to him that if he and the government will take the responsibility for this bill, if he wants to see every fisherman and every mariner thrown on the beach-
How do you make that out?

That is what will happen. My hon. friend does not know; that is the trouble. Under this bill every fisherman in a boat of five ton registry must have a certificate; every marine captain, every man who sails a fishing vessel or a freighter must have a certificate under this foolish, crazy bill, because that is what it is. If my hon. friend and the govern* ment want to take that responsibility, of course I shall lose perhaps $20,000 or $50,000 or $100,000. All right, I can stand that. If my hon. friend wants to be defeated in the next election I shall be willing to sit down right now and pass the bill en bloc.
Yes, what does the hon. member who comes from Toronto care? He was never seasick in his life.
I have travelled hundreds and thousands of miles on the sea and have never been seasick.

The hon. member must have had a good remedy for seasickness. He must have used Mothersill's. This is a serious matter. This bill contains 497 pages; it has been two years in the Senate and it embodies all

the ideas of the Marine department. Of course I admit that the practical men in the Marine department were never consulted about it; the minister cannot deny that.
Are there any there?
Yes, there is Captain Dixon. Was he consulted about this bill? Was Captain Robertson consulted about this bill? No.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know Captain Dixon appeared before the Senate committee and gave all his views on this bill?

My information is that Captain Dixon was not consulted and that Captain Robertson, another practical man in my hon. friend's department, went before the Senate committee on the advice and at the instigation of one of the senators and was refused permission to give information and evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is wrong.
I am not wrong. I am right.

speechtext: He is misinformed.

The Senate is not a hundred miles from this House of Commons, and when any man says in this chamber that he had no opportunity to go before that body he is saying what is not- true and is really convicting himself of a neglect of duty.

Of course I do not mind my hon. friend saying that anything I have said is not true; that is only what I would expect

from him. But I would like him to tell me what he did before the Senate committee, what clauses he got amended and what clauses that he advocated are in this bill?

I got clause 122, paragraph (b) amended, and I got the right of my fishermen to apply for licences to operate their vessels on the waters of lake Winnipeg. I was assisted in that by members of both parties in the upper house. While I am on my feet I want to thank the upper house for the consideration they gave me. Did he give evidence?

Representations were made by organizations from the western coast, from Vancouver and, in fact, the Senate committee was working on May 24 when most of us were away on a holiday. Does my hon. friend not believe it is in this house that he ought to present the case of his electors?
