Listen to this, Mr. Prime Minister:
-of not more than twenty tons gross tonnage.
Is that a steamship? Would he like to cross the Atlantic in one? Would he like to go to the orient in one? Would he like to go anywhere in a steamship of twenty tons gross tonnage?
That is a ship plying in minor waters.

Yes, perhaps it is minor, but the Prime Minister butted into this thing; he butts in when he should allow the Minister of Marine to deal with the matter.
(a)	a steamship of not more than twenty tons gross tonnage, and certificated to carry not more than twelve passengers, plying within specified limits on the minor waters of Canada.
(b)	A steamship of not more than thirty-five tons gross tonnage employed in fishing operations-
Listen to this:
- (including the carrying of fishermen, their wives and children, and fish and fishing supplies used in connection with their operations) plying within specified limits on the inland waters of Canada.
2. The certificate shall describe such steamship and limits. It may be issued for any term not exceeding one year, but may be suspended or cancelled for cause by the minister.
That is all on the statute now.

I am reading the statute or the bill. The hon. member for Selkirk said that he did something in the Senate. I would like to know what he did. Will the hon. member please tell us-and perhaps the Prime Minister will elaborate on this-what happened in the Senate in regard to this clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am going to make only a very few observations, but I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the fact that this bill is a codification of existing
Canada Shipping Act

legislation with such additional clauses as changed conditions between the enactment of the original legislation and its modifications and to-day make necessary. I hear hon. gentlemen talk about the schedules. There are 272 pages of the bill. The first schedule represents the agreement reached at the international Geneva conference which was signed by the late Albert Thomas, director of the International Labour Office, and the late Lord Burnham. That is a matter to which this country gave its approval. The third schedule is the convention concerning the repatriation of seamen, and that too is an international agreement which this country has accepted. This was done in July, 1926, while hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. It is signed by Lord Burnham and Mr. Thomas, late director of the International Labour office, at Geneva. Those two schedules, to both of which this country became a party in July, 1926, are embodied in this bill in accordance with the understanding arrived at that the bill was to contain those provisions.
Then we pass to the fourth schedule which was accepted in 1929 while hon. gentlemen opposite were still in power and Canada was represented, as will be found at page 290, as follows:
The government of Canada:
Mr. Alexander Johnston, Deputy Minister of Marine.
Mr. Lueien Pacaud, secretary in the office of the Canadian High Commissioner in London.
That is the fourth schedule, and it was ratified by parliament last year or the year before.
Put into effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was ratified; it became binding on this dominion. All the clauses do not become effective until the shipping bill is passed. If hon. members follow through the pages they will find all these matters that the house has already ratified or dealt with are in schedule 4. The articles in that schedule number in all sixty-six and the signatures are on pages 324 and 325, our country's signatures being those of Mr. Johnston and Mr. Pacaud.
Then we come to the regulations issued under that schedule. All these regulations ire matters that this house considered and accepted. They are in their very nature technical; they represent an international understanding or agreement. They are not matters that we are enacting for the first time, but they represent, as I have said, an accord or understanding reached between the various countries. For instance, there are
fMr. Bennett.]
the questions of safety at sea and matters of that kind, the form of certificates that are to be issued. On page 373 will be found the second annex dealing with collisions at sea.
Are these not part of this measure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All that has already been accepted by this house.
Are they not part of this measure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the sound signals and matters of that kind are also dealt with in this article. Then you come .to the fifth schedule, page 389. In that instance the government of Canada ivas represented again by Alexander Johnston, deputy minister of Marine. The convention was arrived at in 1930; some hon. members will recall the circumstances in which it was dealt with. That is the load line convention. This house accepted these regulations as international arrangements for the safety of those who travel at sea.
Therefore from page 272 to the end there is nothing that this house has not already accepted. As a matter of fact we are bound internationally by it. Some of the arrangements were made by former administrations, in fact I think it is only fair to say practically all of them; but the regulations were made in part by this administration, as was the duty of this government after they had been agreed to by our representatives. My memory is that the load line convention was agreed to only last year or two years ago.
Now we come to the main part of the bill. It is needless to say that the shipping bill that is the common property of all British peoples was the original shipping act enacted at Westminster. Our shipping act came at a later time and was a modification of that act to the extent necessary to meet our changed conditions. Then when the statute of Westminster was agreed upon, before it had been enacted in fact, in 1926 my hon. friend the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) the Under Secretary for External Affairs, and others including Mr. Read, the counsel of the Department of External Affairs, and Mr. Burchell, of Halifax, met in London and arrived at certain conclusions affecting shipping and other matters. In 1931 the statute of Westminster was enacted. Then it became essential that we should deal with our own shipping act. We did so. It stood. It was considered in the Senate. It stood over. Again it was introduced in the early part of this session and was considered

Canada Shipping Act
with great attention and care. Now what is it? In the main it is a codification of existing legislation, modified by the circumstances to which I have briefly referred. Take the section we are now dealing with, definitions. Is it meet and seemly that this House of Commons should be listening to what we have listened to with respect to this section? This section in the main, with one or two exceptions, has been in force in this country ever since we have had a shipping law.
Will the right hon. gentleman give the sections that have been changed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They are shown in the bill. I am just coming to that. In order that there might be no difficulty in dealing with this matter we have asked that the origin of the sections should be indicated on the page opposite the printed text. It will be found that in respect to the first section, foT instance, attention is directed to the fact that that is section 1, chapter 186, of the revised statutes of Canada.
Now an hon. member has suggested that I have not read the bill. Those of us who attended Dalhousie university will remember the lectures on shipping given by the late Mr. Justice Newcombe, in which we learned that the foundation and basis of Canadian shipping law was the Merchant Shipping Act subsequently embodied in chapter 186 of the revised statutes of Canada.
That is twenty years ago.
Section 1 deals only with the title.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, but what I am pointing out is that the definitions have to be modified by reason of changed conditions.

And the reference is not
given on the opposite page.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, because you could not give a reference to all the definitions; you would have to travel over a very wide radius.
May I interrupt?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

In this section there is
nothing given on the opposite page to show its origin.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, because as I pointed out these are modifications of existing definitions that run through all these acts. In the very nature of things a definitive section can never be said to be already in existence.
My strongest objection is to some of these definitions.
You are going back to the mid-Victorian era.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I said this afternoon, if there is any difficulty in determining whether a definition is adequate, all that has to be done is for hon. gentlemen to say so and that subsection can stand until we have further opportunity to consider it.
That is with regard to the definitions. Now let us commence at part I, of which several of the sections are new. In the very nature of things that must be so, because the changed legislative conditions that have been brought about by our change in status necessitated somewhat different language being employed. Then you have the Merchant Shipping Act, upon which we drew liberally. As everyone knows the effort is to have uniform shipping acts throughout the British Empire, so far as that may be possible.
It cannot be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The provisions are given from which these sections are drawn; you have in every instance a statement of what is new, and if there is any difficulty it is only necessary to state what the difficulty is and it will be dealt with. That is the position. I think in all there are about seventy sections either wholly or partially new, but the arrangement of the sections of course is entirely different in many instances to what it was before, and the grouping and consolidation of sections has been brought about in a manner that it is believed is an improvement as compared with conditions that did exist.
There is nothing difficult or abstruse about this bill except with respect to those matters about which there may be honest differences of opinion. I am not given to suggesting what other men may or may not have done, whether they may or may not have read particular statutes. It is easy to read and not understand; it is easy to read and not be capable of understanding, and there are complicated matters of law
That means me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that it has reference to anyone; I am merely pointing out the fact. Some of these sections have been the subject matter of litigation, and presumably some of them will continue to be such. As I have said, it may be found that there are some differences of opinion with respect to the new sections, but if there are such differences we shall endeavour to
Canada Shipping Act

meet the will of the committee in every reasonable way. If arguments are adduced that indicate there should be some changes made, those changes will be made. To use language that has been used already, the effort is not being made to jam through legislation; rather we are endeavouring to discharge a duty which we owe to the other dominions as well as to ourselves, to get this legislation as perfect as possible in order that there may be some degree of uniformity in shipping legislation having to do with ships that are protected at sea under the British flag. That is the position we are endeavouring to establish. I use the words "British flag" in their broad sense. It may be the mercantile flag of Canada in one case, the flag of the United Kingdom in another, the flag of Australia or of New Zealand in still another.
I do suggest to the committee that it is hardly consonant with our idea of parliament to be talking about sections that we have not yet reached and to be denouncing definitions we have not yet considered. We must remember that parliament has already passed some two hundred pages of this legislation in the form of conventions ir respect to which we sent our representatives to the nations of the world to sign the name of Canada. This parliament subsequently approved those conventions, and we are now endeavouring to give effect to our international word of honour. That is the position.

The Prime Minister admitted that there were seventy sections in this bill which the committee should consider. I am very much afraid that the Prime Minister is back not in the mid-Victorian regime but in the Dalhousie regime of thirty years ago, and that is where the Department of Marine is. This bill is based on a bill which was passed in this country in 1906. The Minister of Marine and the officials who drafted this bill did not know anything about conditions as they are to-day or they never would have included certain clauses that appear in the bill. I can understand, of course, the Prime Minister realizing and appreciating the fact that in the interests of the empire and of everybody else we should try to pass a shipping bill. No one objects to that. I think my right hon. friend will say this much for me, that I am as anxious as he is to have a proper shipping bill in this country, but the trouble is with his Department of Marine.
In this bill we have many clauses from the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain, which are not applicable to Canada, together

with the old clauses of the 1906 bill, which are twenty years behind the times. Who drew this bill? What man in Canada who knows shipping as it is to-day helped to draft this bill? Will the Minister of Marine tell me that? Is there any man who knows what the shipping business means to this country who helped draft this bill? The Minister of Marine cannot answer that question. I say this bill is a conglomeration, a composite of the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain and a bill we had in this country twenty years ago. The Minister of Marine must get up to date. In addition to the seventy clauses the Prime Minister admitted were wrong, which must be amended-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not admit that
anything was wrong. The hon. gentleman surely must have heard what I said.
I did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that.

Did not the Prime Minister
say there were seventy clauses which might be amended?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is open to this committee to amend any clause. I said there were seventy clauses wholly or partially new. The clauses wholly and partially new number about seventy. I am not pretending to give the figure exactly; it may be more or less by two or three, but I think there are thirty-seven of one and thirty-three of the other. It is competent for this committee, of course, to amend them all, but I did not admit that any was wrong. If I had thought so I would have said so at once. I know of none that is wrong.

Well, the Prime Minister is
agreeing with me, except that we do not use the same language. All I said was that all the clauses, except the seventy, were passed in this house in 1906, which was twenty-eight years ago. Surely the Prime Minister must realize that conditions in this country have changed in twenty-eight years. It is all right for somebody down in the marine department who has handled lumber over in Hull or someone who knows nothing about shipping to say that this legislation is all right. They never consulted any man interested in shipping, to have him appear before the Senate committee. I know the Prime Minister, who is interested in this country, will never get up and say that this bill, this monstrosity covering 497 pages, should pass this parliament without the people who are interested in it having something to say about it. Has the Minister of Marine given us any reason

Canada Shipping Act
why this bill should pass? He has not. He read from a telegram from some association in Levis, Quebec. What do they know about this bill? Has the minister consulted the mariners of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick? Has he consulted the captains or mates of Quebec? Has he heard from them? Has he heard from the mariners on the Pacific coast or on the great lakes? He has not, yet here is a bill which took two and a half years in another place. And here is what they got-497 pages of nothing; that is what it is-nothing. They bring it down here on the eighth day of June and, as the Minister of Marine has said, they expect me to read this bill on a Sunday morning, when I should go to the Presbyterian church. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Do you go to church?

I say to the Minister of
Marine that the bill is not fair to the Canadian people. Let him send it to the board of trade of Halifax; let him send it to the board of trade of Yarmouth; let him send it to the board of trade of Lunenburg, or to the board of trade of any other part of the country-Montreal, Quebec, Prince Rupert, or anywhere else; let him send it to those boards of trade; let him ask what they think of this conglomerate bill which does not mean anything, and which will put every mariner who now sails a ship out of business and out on the beach. Is that the objeot of the bill? Surely the Prime Minister does not wish to do that. With all his faults-and I admit that he has not many-he surely does not want to put the fishermen sailing boats over five tons out on the beach. Does he wish to say to a man who without a certificate has sailed a vessel for the last thirty or forty years, "You cannot sail this vessel any more"? If that man does not sail her, who willl sail her? Will the Prime Minister go down and take charge of her? I think quite possibly he could pass the eye test-I know I could not, and the skipper could not. Surely the Prime Minister does not wish to have that condition.
I say this bill could very well stand over until next year, and if at that time the mariners, captains, mates and sailors say there is nothing wrong with it, and if the boards of trade say it is all right, I will be the first man to get up in my place and say, "Mr. Minister of Marine, we will pass this bill in bulk," just as the Senate did, in three minutes. But no one knows what the Senate did with the bill. The only hon. gentleman in this house who had the courtesy to consult me 74726-248
in the matter was the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren). There are several ministers interested in the bill, but the only man who consulted me was the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and he communicated with me through one of his officials. The official consulted me concerning chapter 5, and for several hours we discussed the clauses in that chapter. Speaking modestly may I say it would appear that either the minister of his official had some influence with the committee which sat in another place because I find every suggestion I made is included in chapter 5 of the bill. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Pensions and National Health and to thank him for his courtesy and decency in the matter, because he was the only minister who did so. Of course I admit I do not know much about marine matters, not half as much as people think I know, but the Minister of Pensions and National Health thought I knew something, and as a result he had courtesy enough to consult me. Why did not the Minister of Marine or his officials consult me? Why did they not consult the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), or other hon. members?
Or Charlevoix-Saguenay.

Yes, or the hon. member for
Charlevodx-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain). The only minister who had decency enough to consult anybody on this side of the house was the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I say there is only one proper way in which to deal with the bill: Let the boards of trade of Halifax, Vancouver, Quebec and Montreal have a chance to read it, and if they say they want the fishermen and sailors to be thrown on the beach, then I can stand it as long as the Prime Minister or any other member of his cabinet can stand it.
Carried.

No, it is not carried.
Let me say to the Prime Minister that I am not opposing the enactments approved by this parliament and based on international conventions. On page 273 and following in this enormous bill, schedules are included which, so far as I am concerned, I am perfectly satisfied should be adopted. But I am opposing any hasty decisions on those very conditions the Prime Minister has indicated, namely changes brought about through changed conditions. Every hon. member knows that conditions have changed, and in so far as the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast is concerned they have changed to a very great

Canada Shipping Act

degree. Upon the introduction of this bill changes have been made to the original act under which Canadian shipping has operated for the last twenty-five years, and changes which are extremely detrimental to the present conditions of fisheries in the maritime provinces. I speak about the maritime provinces, because I know whereof I speak, and I am prepared to stand behind anything I say in regard to the conditions under which our fishermen operate, and the conditions necessary for their future welfare.
The hon. member for Selkirk has said he went before the Senate committee and obtained certain amendments. He has stated specifically that an amendment was made to section 122 of the Canada Shipping Act. So as to show the injustice and discrimination contained in the bill against the fishermen on the Atlantic coast I intend to quote the amendment the hon. member has indicated. He may say, "You had the same opportunity as I had to appear before the Senate committee." Mr. Chairman, my reply to that is that I was elected to represent my constituents not in the parliament of Canada but in the House of Commons of Canada, and I am stating that this bill should have been brought down in the House of Commons, the place where the people's representatives would be in a position to place the bill before a committee, such as the one which operated in another place, and upon which such occasion we would have had an opportunity to look into the legislation and to ascertain whether or not amendments were necessary. Then, if that reason is not sufficient, may I say that personally I was not physically able to appear before the Senate or any other committee at that time. However, had I been informed of the injustices contained in the bill I believe I should have come to the conclusion that an attempt should have been made on my part to appear.
To show the injustice of the action taken by another chamber in the construction of the bill, what do I find? I find that they amended section 122 so as to .give special privileges to the fishermen of lake Winnipeg, privileges which should exist for the fishermen on the Atlantic coast.

Would the hon.
member permit a question?
Yes.

Is there not a vast
difference between the conditions existing in connection with fishermen on the inland lakes, and those on the sea?

Yes. I could indicate to the hon. member exactly the same conditions on the Atlantic coast as he claims exist on the inland lakes. Further, I could give a reason why the privileges the hon. gentleman obtained for the inland lakes should exist to a greater degree on the Atlantic coast.
I find that paragraph (b) of section 122 in the bill is as follows:
A steamship of not more than 35 tons gross tonnage employed in fishing operations (including the carrying of fishermen, their wives and children, and fish and fishing supplies used in connection with their operations) plying within specified limits on the inland waters of Canada.
To these steamships certificates may be granted. Does the hon. member for Selkirk mean to tell me that in certain sections of the Atlantic coast we do not require those conditions? What about the islands along the coast? What about carrying our women folk, as is done on the lakes under special privileges, to the lobster factories to help their husbands in carrying on their vocation? What about the carrying of our fishermen in the inland bays and rivers? Our rivers are inland waters just the same as lake Winnipeg and they occupy the same position under this bill. Yet we are not granted that privilege. There is discrimination there. The hon. gentleman was able to go before the committee of the other chamber and have inserted that discrimination against the maritimes. I do not say that he had that in view; I think he had a broader view than that.
Is there anything wrong with the provision? Does not the hon. member want the same provision?

I will answer that when we come to the section. I just want to show the carelessness with which this was considered by the other chamber when the amendment was before it. I may be called down for criticizing the other chamber but I am referring to the committee and I think I am within my rights. When this amendment was suggested to that committee they should have looked over the situation as it affected other waters of the dominion. They should have called in those who had knowledge of the conditions in those other waters which are not inland waters. In that way they would have avoided what I consider to be grave injustice and discrimination against the fishing interests of the maritime provinces. This afternoon the Prime Minister said that I should consider it my duty to represent the whole of Canada when I was in this house. What about the

Canada Shipping Act
hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt)? He so far forgot his duty to the rest of Canada that he went there and had parochial legislation adopted by the Senate committee.
I object to that statement, and I think it ought to be withdrawn. This amendment applies to all inland waters of Canada.
Yes, but it does not apply to the fishing waters of Canada.
Why were not you there? Your whole argument is that I obtained what you wanted to obtain.
What does the hon. member for Selkirk know of the Atlantic or the Pacific? Does he know anything about lake fishing? I doubt it. Did he ever catch a trout or a fish in any of the lakes-or a bullfrog?
I have not got a monopoly of fish or fish stories like my hon. friend.

That is a fishy reply, and it is the only reply the hon. gentleman can make. I stated this afternoon that this bill could very well be left over for another session and that no interests would suffer. In stating that I am in good company. I am in the company of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada. I am in the company of the Minister of Marine. I am in the company of the government of Canada.
You are in bad company.
It may be bad, but I find myself compelled to be in that company for to-night. I hope it will not be for long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is mutual.

I am in the company of this very bill. This bill contains a clause which states that it may be put over. Section 719 reads:
This act shall not come into force until a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette: -
That section gives the minister the power to proclaim only certain clauses and the remainder can be left over.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Not the minister, the governor in council.

The section continues:
-Provided that he may. in the same manner and from time to time, bring any portion or portions only of this act into force.
I am very sincere in fighting this bill. I feel in all conscience that I should oppose it for all I am worth. The suggestion was made
74726-248 J
this afternoon that the government would be prepared to accept amendments which we might suggest. While I know a great deal about the fishing industry I am not prepared to do that without consulting those whose first interest is in that industry. I want to lay this bill before them and discuss it with the men who go down to the sea in ships and who risk their lives night and day in the waters of the maritime provinces to earn a livelihood for themselves and their families and to bring untold wealth to the Dominion of Canada. I want to sit down with those men and go over this bill with them. I want to have their opinions on the effect of this and that clause. I want to come back to this house with that knowledge added to the knowledge I possess already and then suggest to the government what I think is necessary to be enacted to benefit the fishing interests of the Atlantic shores. I am not going to move an amendment to this bill. The government accepts full responsibility for putting it through, and I shall go back to my people and tell them what I did in this house and that the government with its strong majority would not listen to us and put this bill through in spite of us. I can play politics with the next man, and I have enough politics to play against this government without undertaking to use this bill. I consider it my duty to voice my opposition on behalf of my people to anything which will be detrimental to their interests. I come from a nautical family. My father was a sea captain, without a certificate in those days. I have learned from him and from those with whom I have been living for the last fifty years what is in the best interests of the fishermen of the country.
I should like the Prime Minister to listen carefully to a suggestion I intend to make. Under section 719 certain sections of this bill may be proclaimed by order in council. I suggest that the Prime Minister or the government or the Minister of Marine put through such sections of this act as are noncontentious and allow those which we consider to be contentious and detrimental to the people we represent to stand until next session. A bill could be brought in at next session amending the legislation of this year and including such sections as are necessary to help the fishermen whom we represent in this house. I hope the Prime Minister will consider that suggestion.

I was hoping that either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Marine would see the reasonableness of the argument put forward by the hon. member for Glou-
Canada Shipping Act

cester (Mr. Veniot) but if we are going to consider section 2, although we have carried subsection 1 of section 2, I would like to ask the minister what subsection 1 really means. It says:
"The Admiralty" means the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom for the time being, or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom.
We are an independent nation, perhaps not a nation, but at all events an independent country; why should we be under the sovereignty of the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom? Why should the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom appear in this bill a shipping act of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend when reading the bill must have seen that the word "Admiralty" is mentioned in certain parts, so we had to define "Admiralty." That is all.

That is not quite sufficient, Mr. Chairman. "Admiralty court" is defined in subsection 2. I can understand that, but what I am asking the minister is why this Dominion of Canada should be under the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom. How does that come in, in this country? I can understand that there would be references to the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain, but as for the Lord High Admiral, we have none; I am the only admiral in this country. Why therefore does the Lord High Admiral appear in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have already told my hon. friend that we refer to the Admiralty in certain parts of this bill and so in the definition section we define "the Admiralty." There is no harm in that.

I do not say that there is any harm in it. I have not had a chance to study this bill, although the Lord knows I have done the best I could. Of course, I admit I am stupid, I admit I am slow, I admit I am ignorant, I admit it is impossible for me in my ordinary capacity to study a bill of 497 pages in four days despite the fact that after I came home from the Presbyterian church on Sunday morning I spent the rest of the day trying to wade through these 497 pages. I took the minister's advice, and although I did not go to high mass on Sunday morning I went to the eleven o'clock service at the Presbyterian church, and as soon as I got home I sat down with this bill. I am sure the Prime

Minister will sympathize with me, because he is quite a religious man like myself, when I tell him that all I could get through on Sunday was seventy-four pages. The Prime Minister goes to Chalmers church and I go to Knox church, but I will bet dollars to doughnuts that the Prime Minister did not read this bill on Sunday like I did. He is too sincere: he does not believe in doing business on Sunday. But the Minister of Marine had asked us to read the bill over the week-end and so I waded through it and I got only as far as page 74. I have had the bill now for a week and the best I have been able to do was to get to page 74, section 174.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That is more than half of the bill.
No. There are 719 clauses. The minister has not read the bill. He has not looked at it. He does not know what it is all about. There are 719 sections-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Over 700 sections.

I want to keep the minister right on this. He is trying to get this thing into his head but it is impossible because he does not know anything about marine matters. There are 497 pages in this bill and all I have got through so far is to page 74, in spite of the fact that I spent all Sunday till twelve o'clock at night reading this bill.
Did you have supper?

Yes, a seventy-five cent supper at the Alexandra, after sticking at the bill from twelve to six o'clock and going over seventy-four pages.
I congratulate the minister on the fact that he has been able, as he has told us, to go through this bill, but I want to say to him that it is not fair to bring a bill of this importance and extent to parliament in the last days of the session and ask us to pass it in its present condition. The minister cannot show to this committee that any board of trade or any organization whether of seamen or of master mariners or of fishermen has asked that this bill should pass this session. It has taken the Senate two years to deal with this bill, and I am not reflecting at all on the other chamber in the eastern portion of this building. But why does the Prime Minister force the Minister of Marine to come here and ask that we pass the bill this session? Of course, if the Prime Minister and the government want to commit suicide, if they want to put this bill through, well and good.

Why should you object if they commit suicide?
I would not like to see the Prime Minister commit suicide.
I mean politically.

It is too serious. I am not playing politics in this thing at all. Let me refer to chapter 2, if I remember correctly. That chapter, I want to say to the Prime Minister, should be revised in its entirety. The trouble with the minister-not the minister; I should have said with his officials who advised him in this matter, and I apologize- the trouble with his officials is that they are twenty-five years behind the times. They are living in the mid-Victorian era or in the time of King Henry VIII.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned chapter 2. There is no chapter in the bill. Does he mean pant II?

That is splitting hairs, Mr. Chairman. The minister is sailing close to the wind for a man w'ho is a lawyer in Montreal. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister could luff a little and tack on the other side.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is proceeding under auxiliary power.
Then he puts his sails down.
Or double reefs.

The Minister of Marine should not talk that way to an old sea lawyer like myself from the maritime provinces. It is not right for a lawyer from an inland town like Montreal to criticize an old sea lawyer like myself for referring to chapter 2 instead of part II.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is because my hon. friend had not mentioned the section and I wanted to know to what part he referred.

I appreciate my hon. friend's
lack of knowledge with regard to this whole matter and am delighted he has drawn my attention to the fact. I am not saying this in a disparaging manner to my hon. friend because I realize he is placed in a very awkward position. For two years another part of this parliament has dealt with this matter and it has been forced on the Minister of Marine. If he and I got together for two or three hours, we could splice the main brace and discuss this matter.
That is a good suggestion.

Wait till the sun gets
over the foreyard arm.

We might do that. Still, the
Minister of Marine does not want to force on this country a bill which as drafted is a conglomerate measure, a bill which mixes up clauses of the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain with chapter 186 of the revised statutes of Canada. Surely he does not want to go down in history as the man who put a bill through this parliament just because we are here now on the twelfth day of June and because the measure was passed by the Senate which had no interest in it. There was not a man on the Senate committee who invited anybody there who knew anything about the bill. Who were the witnesses? Will the Minister of Marine tell me who came before that Senate committee? I am not deprecating the work of the right hon. leader of the Senate nor of any other member of the Senate, but I say to the Minister of Marine that the real shipping people, the fishermen, the mariners, the sailors of this country, the business men, never saw this bill, never had an opportunity to go before the Senate and have not an opportunity now to express their views in regard to the matter.
I have no political axe to grind in connection with this question. I was born with a fishbone in my mouth, born by the sea, brought up with fishermen, mariners, sailors. Surely the minister does not want to say that I am playing politics in regard to this, because I am not. I am a Grit, of course, and I am a free trader. I am opposed to this government but I am not opposed to this legislation because it is brought down by this government. I say that it is too serious a matter to deal with hastily; it is a business matter, one that affects practically every man, woman and child in Canada, that affects every sailor, every seaman, every master, every mate, every shipping interest and every business interest in this dominion, because under this measure they will be responsible for what they do in regard to every cargo that is loaded.
Let the boards of trade, masters and mates, seamen, come back here after they read this bill or send their representations and say whether it is a good one or not. If they say that it is all right, so far as I am concerned I shall accept it. In the last four days I have sent seventeen copies of this measure out to people in Nova Scotia. Will my hon. friend say that I have had any opportunity to receive replies? I sent seventeen copies to different parts of the maritime provinces and I want those people, whether the chamber of com-
Canada Shipping Act

merce of Yarmouth, or Halifax, or Lunenburg, or Canso, or Sydney, to give me their replies. I want the boards of trade of those towns to consult the captains, seamen and anybody else interested, and I say to the minister: Why force this bill through now? Nobody is asking for it. I say in all seriousness that in the last three months I have not had one word asking me to approve this or any shipping bill. The people concerned are quite satisfied with the old act because if this new legislation is put into force thousands of fishermen, thousands of sailors and, Mr. Chairman, hundreds in your own constituency of Cumberland, men who have sailed the seas for thirty, or twenty, or ten years, will be thrown on the beach. Is it fair that this party or this government or this parliament should say to the men of Cumberland, of Guysborough and of other places throughout Nova Scotia: You cannot sail your ships?
Does that not break your heart, Mr. Chairman?

Yes, it does, because he knows I am right. Is it fair to men who have sailed the seas to Brazil, Hawaii, Rio de Janeiro, that they should be thrown on the beach through this stupid and foolish bill drawn by my hon. friend and by men who never saw salt water? The technical, practical men in the Department of Marine were never consulted about this bill. Who is there in the Senate who knows about the bay of Fundy, the Atlantic or the Pacific ocean? Yet not a practical man was consulted and I say in all seriousness: I do not care; I can stand this if the government can stand it, but heaven knows what is going to happen to them at the next election. If, however, they are going to put this bill through, I am satisfied; let them do it.

When talking a little while ago on the amendment made to section 112 of chapter 186 I forgot lo point out that under the former act temporary certificates were permitted for vessels of less than ten tons, propelled by sail and auxiliary engine. Under this amendment in one instance that provision is extended to vessels of twenty tons and in another to vessels of thirty-five tons, for inland waters, whereas in the coastal service it is confined to vessels with auxiliaries of not over three horsepower; anything above that is classified as a steamer, and full certificates must be obtained for mates and masters. This applies to vessels in our fishing fleet having auxiliaries; although they are in one sense classified as sailing vessels, under this bill they

become steamers when their auxiliary is over three horsepower. Yet on the inland lakes it extends to vessels of twenty and thirty-five tons, which require a great deal more than three horsepower auxiliaries to navigate them. They are given that privilege, but we on the Atlantic coast are discriminated against in that way.

There is no doubt whatever that this bill is very much needed. Some of the penal sections of the present act are expressed in terms of pounds, shillings, and pence, which indicates its old origin. I think there was a bill drawn in 1908 or 1909, but for some reason which I have not been able to discover it never was brought into the house. It is perfectly true that members on this side including myself have been worrying the minister for years to introduce an amendment to the act. We have no quarrel with the idea that it is needed; it is only with the manner of its introduction that we find any fault.
Now, it is said that there are not many sections. Even taking the' minister's own statement that there are only seventy new sections, that is a considerable bill. However it might not be so serious if it were one readily understood by ordinary members of parliament. But it is not; in some aspects it is highly technical and impossible to discuss intelligently on the floor of this house, and that is why I have always urged that it should be considered in a committee where technical  men can come before us and we could have these questions explained. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) said that we should have gone and listened to the discussions in the Senate committee-*

I said I attended them;
I did not make any suggestion to others.
He was setting a good example.

The hon. member was not suggesting that he did wrong in going there;
I think his suggestion was an open invitation to go and do likewise, as in the biblical example. I did not go myself; for one thing I did not know when the committee was sitting, and I have something else to do than attend committee meetings in another house;
I have enough to do to attend our own. But I did attend another committee on another occasion when, as the hon, member said, I was treated courteously and heard patiently.
I was allowed to make a statement, but I was not allowed to sit in and question witnesses or pass opinions. It would be indecorous; it

Canada Shipping Act
is not done. But I did the next best thing, as I thought; I sent for the evidence taken before that special committee-it was referred to a special committee and a subcommittee.
I sent for the evidence in order that I might inform myself as to the numerous witnesses who according to the minister had given substantial and worthy evidences The answer was: there was no evidence; nothing had been printed. So how could we inform ourselves?
I do not know that anyone gave evidence.
I will take the minister's word that some did, but I do not know who they were; I do not know if they were making ex parte statements in their own interest or in the interest of the class they represent. I know nothing to guide me in deciding whether this bill is a suitable bill or not.
I think the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) would not take it amiss if I say that he is very strong on constitutional points. I wonder that he or someone has not taken up this constitutional point, that it does not become us to subordinate our rights of legislation to another chamber. Not that we should be jealous of our dignity, or touchy-not at all; but we should be jealous, and I propose to be, of the rights delegated to us by the people at the last election. They sent us here to represent them in passing legislation, not to accept legislation originating in another chamber, and swallow it holus-bolus and say that because it has received approval there we should just attach our signatures. That method was tried in the case of the railway bill a year ago, but we changed that bill in practically every detail. I think it is not the custom for the British House of Lords to introduce legislation of any substantial nature but to have it submitted with all formality to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The rule is that legislation involving public expenditure originates in the Commons. Much important legislation has in times past originated in the Lords. Of the practice at the moment I cannot speak.

Not of late years, I think;
it has fallen into desuetude. Public opinion has insisted that the House of Commons is the responsible body, and I for one do not propose to subordinate its powers to any other chamber, however honourable or worthy it may be.
Then we were told that we should have read the bill. It is not impossible to read it, but that would not do us much good. I do not say this bill is wrong; I say I do not know, because there are many features of it on which I cannot form an opinion without
technical advice, and there is none obtainable in this chamber. Here is a letter I received -true, it was a year ago-in connection with the bill very similar to this, then before the Senate. I sent it to the Canadian Association of Seamen in Vancouver. Here is part of their reply:
For three weeks we have had a committee working steadily on each clause, and on rereading the amendments I am of the opinion that we have introduced one or two contradictory clauses, but to make our reading more easily understood, I am enclosing herewith a few comments relative to said amendments.
The few comments consist of four closely typewritten pages, and the original amendments that they suggest make thirty-two closely typewritten pages. They say that having their interests at heart they have had a committee steadily working on it for three weeks; yet we are going to railroad it through by just looking at it and someone reading out some word on the margin like "wharf" 'or "wreck" and so passing that particular section.
Then I have a letter this year submitting on three pages perhaps thirty suggestions, some of them of a very technical character. I read one the other night and I shall not repeat it, but it is not one on which we could form an estimate without having a technical man before us.
I come back to what I have been urging for the last two years; why not send it to a committee, not necessarily the marine committee, but to a special committee? I believe even yet it would be possible to do it, and in so doing it would get through a lot quicker than by trying to put it through this house in this manner. But the better way would be to leave it for another year and bring it down to the committee early in the session; then we would have the advantage of experience during the recess and could deal with it in an adequate way. My own view is that if the government decide to go on with it

the Prime Minister objects to the term "jamming it through," but I cannot think of any more appropriate term-if they decide to force it through, then I think my attitude should be to wash my hands of it and say that I cannot adequately advise, and the responsibility before the people must be theirs. It is absolutely certain that the bill is not perfect, from the complaints I have here and the number of clauses. I think the proper course would be not to lay ourselves open to the charge of obstructing-we do not want to do that-but simply to say "your blood be on your own head" as far as results are concerned.

Just after eight o'clock I asked the Minister of Marine whether any personal representations had been made by the Canadian Association of Seamen. My reason for asking that is that the bill has, I believe, 131 clauses pertaining to seamen alone. The greater part of this deals with the very life of the seaman, his property, what happens to him if he gets sick, his wages, his dismissal, what is done if he gets stranded on a foreign shore, his certificate .of competency, and everything pertaining to his life on the ship and off it.
Hear, hear.
It touches the very life of the seaman, yet no personal representations were made on his behalf in the Senate.
Not one.

I shall not say they would not have been allowed, but they were not represented when it was before the Senate committee. I must object also to the implication or even the suggestion that a member is derelict in his duty because he does not appear before a Senate committee. I think that would be a bad precedent, especially during this session when there were so many committees in operation. But referring to those 131 sections I doubt if there is any man in this house in a position to know all the conditions affecting seamen. Now that the bill is being put into a new form it should not only be brought up to date but the seamen should be represented before the committee dealing with these matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All those sections were there before.

I quite agree, and I am glad the Prime Minister mentioned that. One of the complaints made by the seamen was that it was very difficult to get amendments made to the old act. It has been stated that the bill has been copied. That being so it is behind the times. If one looks through the bill he will find the term "steamship," alone used, as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) suggested, but the change to motor power has been omitted. That alone shows that the bill needs revision.
Carried?
No, it is not going to carry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By the definition, "steamship" covers a motor ship.

That is the trouble. The government does not seem to realize that a motor boat should not be classed as a steamer.
Mr. Neill.]
A moment ago I asked the minister why subsection 1 of section 2 should be in this bill. Why should the Admiralty or the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom appear in this bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I answer that
question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Admiralty is referred to in this bill, and the definition of the word is the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom for the time being, or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom. If you have any word to which a meaning attaches in the statute it is desirable to define what that meaning is, according to the country which has that word in its statutes for expressing a given meaning. The meaning assigned to this word is the meaning assigned to it under the laws of Great Britain, and when it is used here it has that meaning.

I quite understand that
definition, but I want to know why that should appear in a Canadian statute and where those words are used in the 497 pages of the bill. I have gone through only 74 pages, but I cannot find any reference to the Lord High Admiral -unless it is myself-of the United Kingdom for the time being or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral. I can understand, of course, that we look after our own affairs, that we are daughter in our mother's house but mistress in our own. Is that the correct quotation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is.

I am a great Britisher; I believe only one flag should fly over the empire, but in a Canadian shipping bill why should this subsection be inserted in the definitions when, in the 74 pages I have examined, I can find no reference to the Lord High Admiral, whether it is Winston Churchill or someone else, or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office? I want to know from the minister why that definition is there when no reference is made to the Lord High Admiral in the 497 pages of the bill, as far as I can tell.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend does not affirm that there is no mention of the Admiralty in the whole bill?

I did not say that. That shows conclusively that the minister is more at sea than I am; in fact he is in heavy weather. I

Canada Shipping Act
am sailing along with all sails set, with the gaff topsails and the balloon jib and everything else going. The minister Iras his sails reefed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why don't you drop your sea anchor?
Not while the ship is under sail. You only drop the anchor when you are getting near the breakers or the shore. The Prime Minister should tell the Minister of Marine to drop his anchor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said your sea anchor; there is a great difference.
It is used only in a gale of wind-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the point.
-when you put your anchor out to keep your head in the wind. The Prime Minister and I are going to get seasick if we continue this discussion.
The Prime Minister means to heave to.

That is not heaving to. My
hon. friend is a lawyer; for heaven's sake don't let us get into an argument. You heave to with only your foresail set. You are jogging to windward when you pull your jib to windward.
I want to know why subsection 1 appears in this bill. The minister says he has read the bill; he says he did not go to mass on Sunday because he was studying the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
joking. I never said any such thing.

At any rate the minister said he did not go to mass last Sunday. Will he tell me why subsection 1 of section 2 is included in this bill, when we are in a free country and we are talking about a Canadian statute? I could understand it if the government wanted to give me a higher title than I have already and call me the lord high admiral instead of just admiral. I would be satisfied; I would take the title whether it came on the king's birthday or at any other time. But where does that appear in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend
any objection to that definition?
I am asking for an explanation.

This subsection has been carried. It
is the only one that has been carried, and it seems to me this discussion is out of order.

We had an understanding the other night with the Minister of Finance, who is a very good friend of mine, that we would pass that subsection in order that the business of the house might go on, with the understanding that when the bill came up- if it did, because we hoped that the Minister of Finance would have sufficient influence, being a sailor from the maritime provinces and knowing the shipping business as he does, to see that it did not come up until next session'-we would have an opportunity to discuss anything we desired. Since the bill has come up I should like to ask why this subsection appears in the bill. Where is it referred to? The minister says he has read and understands the bill. Surely as a matter of courtesy it would be very simple for him to tell me where this subsection is referred to in any other part of this terrible bill which on account of its bulk I can hardly hold in my hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: When my hon. friend arrives at the section he will see where the Admiralty is mentioned.

The Admiralty is mentioned
in subsection 2. I understand what an admiralty court means, of course, because I have been before it half a dozen times. I should like to know why the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom should interfere in Canadian shipping.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He does not; it is a
definition of the word.

Surely it means something; if
it does not it should not be there. I want the minister to tell me what it means and where it applies in the 497 pages of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That subsection was
carried on Friday last, and my hon. friend is too inquisitive to let this subsection go without discussion this evening. When we started to discuss this bill in committee I began with section 1. Hon. gentlemen opposite objected, because that was the only section that would allow them to say anything at all on the bill. So I left that section aside and began with section 2, subsection 1, which was adopted without any reservation whatever.
What are we discussing?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
At the beginning the chairman of the committee stated that the hon. gentleman was absolutely out of order in the discussion he has been carrying on this evening.

He has been out of order for an hour and a half; I think he should see the Minister of Health again.

I am afraid the Minister of Marine is losing his temper. I am trying to be as respectful to him and to the government as I can be. I believe the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine should agree with me when I say we allowed the second reading of the bill. Then, I was prepared to consent to the carrying of clause 1, but the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) thought the clause should not be passed, and with the consent of the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Finance we went on with clause 2. We passed subsection 1 of section 2 merely as a matter of courtesy to the government and to the minister. Surely it does not lie in the mouth of the Minister of Marine to eay that I am inquisitive. I am not inquisitive ; I say that the minister does not know where in these 497 pages to find the words "Lord High Admiral," and he cannot indicate a reference to any such person. When he knows he cannot make such reference, and when he knows that the definition means nothing, he should be more courteous. We have before us a bill which affects Canadian shipping, and as is well known this country has no lord high admiral, and it has no commissioners for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom. Why should that subsection be in the bill? The fact that it is in the bill shows conclusively that the minister and the officials who drafted the bill, the gentlemen responsible for it, did not give it sufficient and careful attention. I say that subsection 1 should be expunged from the bill, and I suggest that the minister is not acting wisely when he states that I am too inquisitive. I have too much interest in the bill to be accused in that way. I suggest he has no justification for saying I am inquisitive because I want to know where, in these 497 pages, there is any reference to the Lord High Admiral. The minister states he has read the bill and that he knows all about it. Certainly the officials sitting near him should know something about it. Let him tell me where the Lord High Admiral comes into this Canadian shipping legislation. Will the minister tell me the page, the clause or appendix? He cannot tell me, and yet he says that I am too inquisitive.

The ruling of the chair is that this subsection has passed. If by unanimous con-

sent the house wishes to go back and discuss the paragraph, I have no objection. My record shows however that the subsection has been passed.
Is there a lord high admiral in Cumberland county?

We must
interpret the words "the Admiralty" by the definition appearing in the subsection. The hon. member is simply asking why the words appear.
Shall the subsection carry?

Apparently the Minister of
Marine cannot find any place where subsection 1 refers to the bill under discussion. I am surprised that to-night the Minister of Marine takes a different attitude from the one he took on Friday night, upon which occasion we had a very agreeable discussion in which the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Finance, who is now leaving the chamber, took part. On Friday evening I referred in a joking manner to this particular subsection, and I thought the Minister of Finance understood the joke. Then, following my remark I find that at page 3825 the Minister of Finance is reported as follows:
The suggestion of the lord high admiral of the opposition is entirely acceptable. I can assure my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni that there was no idea in the mind of the government to take any advantage, either technical or otherwise, in calling the first section of the bill. I submit that the rights of the house and the committee are preserved in precisely the same manner whether the section is passed or not passed, but I accept without question the suggestion of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The Minister of
Finance mentioned section 1.

We were discussing the advisability of helping the government to go on with this legislation, and we agreed to pass the second reading and to go into committee. I think the Minister of Finance will agree with me that there were no strings on what we did. We took the action which is taken in many other instances, whether they be public works measures, or anything else, whereby for the sake of convenience to the government the opposition allows a section to pass, with the understanding that the section may be reopened or discussed when the bill comes up again.
All I am asking the minister is this, and if he cannot answer me, I merely wish him to say so: Why in a bill introduced to this parliament of Canada, a free country which can

Canada Shipping Act
pass its own legislation, should we include such definitions? It would seem to indicate that the advisers of the minister and of the Senate, those high priced lawyers from Vancouver and the other place, did not know what the bill meant, when they included subsection 1 of section 2 in its provisions. Of course, it was a matter of $100 a day or nothing. It was an easy matter to take the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain, it was an easy matter to take the statutes of Canada, and to make a composite act.
And to take a pair of scissors and a bottle of paste.

Yes, a pair of scissors and a
paste brush. That was a very easy matter for $100 a day. The Minister of Marine knows very well that that is what happened.
I am not reflecting upon what took place in the southeast corner of this building. I am not objecting to a Tory getting a good job when this government is in power. If I were in power again I would get good jobs for my friends, if I could. I say to the minister that he should not accept a bill affecting the rights, property and business of seamen, sailors, captains, mates and property owners, which came only five days ago from another corner of this building, and then bring it into this chamber and expect us to pass the bill without consulting our constituents, the people in Canada, the boards of trade or the shipping interests. I allowed subsection 1 to pass and hon. members on this side of the house allowed it to pass merely as a matter of courtesy to the government and to my good friend the Minister of Finance. Surely you, sir, or the Minister of Marine should not now say that I should not object to subsection 1 because upon another occasion I thought the words might be used in the bill. However, since that time I have tried to go through the bill; as I say I spent Sunday-and I know as a good Presbyterian I should not have done it-from one o'clock in the afternoon until twelve o'clock at night in a perusal of the bill. I accepted the advice offered by the Prime Minister. I got up in the morning, and after going to church studied the bill from one o'clock until twelve o'clock at night-and I don't know what my wife will say when she hears about it. I did that, and I am serious when I say to hon. members opposite that I have no political axe to grind in opposing the measure. This bill means the livelihood of men with whom I have been associated for the last forty yearn. Is the Minister of Marine going to say that he will force this bill through? Will the Prime Minister say
that, after the promises and the fine speeches he made in -the maritime provinces when he was down there in 1930? How will he face them in October, or some time this fall when he calls an election? Can he face the fishermen and the masters, mates, etc., who will be thrown out on the beach, and out of employment? I am just as serious as I possibly can be in this matter. I would not be standing here attacking this bill if I was not serious.
I do not object to the Senate sending us this bill as it now is; they did the best they could.
I contend that the boards of trade and the shipping interests, the business interests, the fishermen, the seamen, the sailors and the master mariners who are affected by this bill, should be heard. The Minister of National Health was the only member of the government who showed me the courtesy of consulting me. He consulted with me in reference to the poor devils who have to go to hospitals. This is an important bill as it affects not only captains and mates, but seamen, engineers, fishermen, pilots and everyone else. I say to the Minister of Marine: Let us let this bill stand over. No one will be hurt. I am sure the minister will agree with me that if there was any desire that this bill should be passed, I would have heard something about it. Could I afford to stand up here and oppose the passing of this bill if I had received petitions or letters from the shipping interests of this country asking that it be passed? Certainly I could not. Of course, the joke is that I do not know as much about shipping as people think I do, but I do not want to lose that reputation. I have not received one word asking that this bill be passed. No one has seen it. It is all right for someone whom nobody knows to come here from somewhere, but I think my hon. friend must admit that no really practical men appeared before the Senate committee. The only ones who appeared were those who wanted some special privileges. My hon. friend knows that the people interested in shipping on the great lakes are opposed to certain sections of this bill. I am not opposed to those sections personally, but as a man who has some interest in the shipping of this country, I feel I must oppose them. I opposed a bill when the liberal party was in power some twelve or fifteen years ago, and it was held over. This bill was opposed last year; it was never proclaimed because the Prime Minister realized-he will pardon me for saying this-that the bill was not practical. The bill which I opposed some twelve or fifteen years ago when the Liberal party was in power did not do any good to my party.
