I am serious in this. I say to the Prime Minister, I say to the government and I say to the Minister of Marine: Nobody will be hurt by letting this bill stand until next session. As I said a moment ago, I have sent seventeen copies of this conglomerate bill to my friends but it will take them at least two months to study it properly. Let us let this thing go over until next year. I say to the Minister of Marine and to the Prime Minister: Surely there are certain interests in this country which should be protected. There is no necessity to pass this and we cannot pass it. I cannot afford to stand here and let this thing go through as it is unless I am willing to let the government and the Prime Minister take the responsibility. The Minister of Trade and Commerce cut out the subsidies for steamers and many of these men have had to go on sailing vessels. Now the captains of such vessels of over five tons having auxiliary power must have certificates. These men cannot get certificates. I shall not give the reasons why just now, but I will if we are forced to deal with chapter 2. I am not playing politics in this, I am talking for the shipping and business interests of this country. I am not objecting to what the Senate did; -I am not objecting to the government putting this bill in the Senate; all I am saying is that the fishermen, the sailors, the pilots, the seamen and everyone else should have a chance to look at this bill. They should have an opportunity to discuss this matter with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Stanley), the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall), the hon. member for Cape Breton-North Victoria (Mr. Johnstone) and the hon. members from Vancouver. I am as much interested as anybody in seeing that the regulations for the safety of shipping at sea are carried out, but I ask that this bill be allowed to stand over so that those who are interested may be heard before next session. If there is no objection by next session, I will be ready to put this bill through in the shortest possible time.

I should like to say a
word with regard to what the Prime Minister said in connection with uniformity of legislation. He spoke of the necessity for having this legislation in order to promote uniformity among the dominions. As he correctly said, the history of this legislation is that in 1929 there was a conference on dominion shipping legislation and merchant shipping legislation. The result of that conference was a report which was presented to the imperial confer-

ence of 1930. That report recommended an agreement on uniform shipping legislation throughout the empire and an agreement was arrived at and was approved at the 1930 conference and signed in 1931. This agreement laid down the general principles of the uniform legislation and it, of course, contemplated that there would be legislation following the laying down of those principles. I submit that that legislation cannot be uniform unless there is a further conference between the various members of the British commonwealth of nations. It seems to me that we can hardly have uniformity if we start out by passing a Canada Shipping Act all by ourselves and expecting the other dominions to follow. My view is that we would be doing more in the way of uniformity if we held a conference with the other dominions and then passed an act modelled along the lines suggested at that conference.
That is what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) suggested on Friday night.

As I understand it, what we have at the present time is general uniformity from the fact that the Merchant Shipping Act is in force all over the British commonwealth. Then all the various dominions have are their own local shipping acts. We have the Canada Shipping Act here. I am told that the hon. member for Pictou has already suggested such a conference and I am convinced that it would be in the interests of uniformity if we did not start off by attempting to lead the procession, as it were, by passing an act and expecting the other dominions to rubber stamp what we do. That is my first point. My right hon. friend has mentioned that there is some sort of pledge, that we have passed our word of honour.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was dealing with international obligations.

I do not think we would
be violating any word of honour, and I do not believe my right hon. friend intended that his remarks should be so interpreted, by not passing this shipping bill. This bill is made up by the use of the pastepot and by the redrafting of legislation which was already in force. I imagine it was done in both ways. Then in addition to reenacting the old legislation it contains some new legislation. I submit that we cannot hope to have the sort of shipping legislation we should have in this country if we just follow the old British Merchant Shipping Act and our own Canada Shipping Act. The Merchant Shipping Act was originally passed in 1854

Canada Shipping Act
before the days of cables, before the days of radio, before the days of aircraft and before the days of various modern aids to navigation. The result is that the Merchant Shipping Act is bound to be to some extent out of date. Amendments have been passed from time to time but no one believes that that aot has had the overhauling which it needs in order to make it completely in keeping with present conditions. The delay in doing this has been due to the fact that the various dominions have, following the statute of Westminster, been considering the best way to bring about uniformity in shipping legislation. I submit that notwithstanding all the work that has been done, and I find no fault with the work that has been done in drafting the act, we shall not have an up to date act when we get through with this if we simply adopt the Merchant Shipping Act and fit into it the Canada Shipping Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We have to.
That brings me to my next point. As I understood the Prime Minister, he was suggesting first that we should pass this bill, because it contains what is already on the statute books.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I said there were seventy new sections.

Dealing with the law that is on the statute books. Why should we pass this act simply to reenact what is already on the statute books? It is there now and we have the benefit of it. It seems to me that we can afford to wait until we bring our shipping legislation into line with that of the other commonwealths before we decide on a brand new act. That is, so far as the legislation which is already in force is concerned, we are not going a step further ahead by rewriting it on the statute books.
My right bon. friend says there are seventy-five new sections. But even some of the old ones can hardly be recognized. I just look at one section, section 113. I know very little about shipping law; I do not profess to have made a close study of it. I have to learn in this school if we have to go through with this bill. Section 113 deals with shipping registry. Apparently that section is a combination of sections 93, 94, 95, 96 and 97 of the old Canada Shipping Act. You will not find it written in the same berms. I would not expect that. I would expect the draftsman to improve on it. But imagine those of us in this committee attempting to figure out whether it contains the old legislation or whether it is a
brand new section. That is just one sample. That is a section which my right hou. friend the Prime Minister would include under present existing legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, partly new.

Partly new, all right; but as I understand the principle, it is intended to be practically the same as the old legislation. In addition my right hon. friend says that there are seventydive new sections. That brings me to this.
Section 113 is not new.

My hon. friend from
Antigonish-Guysborough says that section 113 is not new. I aim taking his word and the word of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and assuming that the principle of it generally is already in force and that the drafting of it is new. Now about the new sections? What I am suggesting to my right hon. friend is this: We dealt with the companies act this session and adopted a number of amendments. I do not think my right hon. friend will complain of the way in which we on this side of the house dealt with that bill.
I do noit think he will complain of the way in which we dealt with about ten other pieces of legislation which have come before the house this session. The only bill that has really been contentious and taken a long time was the marketing act. The other bills have had all the expedition that my right hon. friend could possibly expect, and I am quite satisfied that he will frankly admit that. We had last night the bill dealing with compromises in the matter of farm indebtedness. We have dealt with a farm loan bill, a British and foreign companies insurance act, a Canadian insurance act; a tremendous bill consisting of a remodelling and revision of the Excise Act, and the companies act, which I have just mentioned. Then we have had the complete decennial revision this session of the Bank Act. We have also had the bill to incorporate the central bank of Canada, and in addition the Fruit Act, the Food and Drug Act, the Bills of Exchange Act, and the Admiralty Court Act. We have dealt with all that legislation this session, and now at this late date we are asked to deal with this monumental bill of 497 pages. I submit to my right hon. friend that we are having a surfeit, a gorge of legislation which we cannot possibly digest.
I say to him that with regard to this act we should deal with it as we dealt with the companies act, and have it go to a committee and consider the sections, see what the seventy-five new sections contain, and if the
Canada Shipping Act

committee can agree on the sections, well and good; but I submit to my right hon. friend that it is very difficult and not the most efficient way to do public business for us to attempt in this committee of the whole to deal with 719 sections, new and old, without an opportunity at least for a preliminary digest of the situation in a committee. I want to ask my right hon. friend even yet, if he will not agree to this bill being referred to a special committee which would have an opportunity to go over it, and if we find that it is not possible to deal with it properly before this session rises, the bill will simply have to stand over until next session. I submit to my right hon. friend that the way we have already dealt with legislation ought to induce him to accept a suggestion of this kind and to make him feel that there is no desire whatever to obstruct this legislation, but that there is on the other hand a real desire on the part of the committee to know something about the legislation which they are passing.
I do not think my right hon. friend any more than anybody else will say that simply because of the fact that the Senate has passed the bill and given it a lot of attention, that is any reason why we should not give it proper consideration in this house. The other chamber had all last year to consider this bill; they scrapped practically the whole of the bill which was drawn, and started out on a brand new bill this year, and now after nearly three months' work this bill is brought down to us. I submit to my right hon. friend that it is very difficult for us to deal with it in this way. It is not a practical way to deal with it, and I ask him in all earnestness if he will not consider the possibility, even at this stage, and before we go ahead with the various sections of the bill, of referring it to a committee.
Let me say to him that if we do pass the bill in the form in which it is we shall not have an opportunity for a number of years properly to revise and bring the bill up to date. We shall have put on record a bill that is more or less permeated with the atmosphere of the legislation which has existed since 1854. We shall probably overlook some vital features in connection with modern navigation and shipping. I think we could have taken care of these things if we applied ourselves to it by taking up a brand new, up to date body of shipping legislation as concurred in by all the other dominions, and I think it would be well for us to wait another year in order to do it.

One last word, and it is this. This is the first piece of legislation that we shall have passed, I think, since the statute of Westminster; I mean directly as a result of it. We have passed trade agreements from time to time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And the Naturalization Act, and the Oath of Allegiance Act.

The Oath of Allegiance Act was a comparatively formal matter, and the Naturalization Act we had dealt with pretty fully before the statute of Westminster. But this is a new departure. For the first time we are passing our own shipping legislation exclusively; doing away with what has been the charter of the seamen's liberty, namely, the Merchant Shipping Act. We are attempting to put on the Canadian statute books what was previously on the British statute books and adopting that as our own. I think we can afford, although it is four years since the statute of Westminster was passed, to go slowly in this respect. This is all-important legislation, affecting not only the sea coasts of this country, but mercantile interests right across Canada. So far as I am personally concerned I would like to see this legislation go through, but if it is impossible to deal with it competently this session I would ask my right hon. friend, first, to consider leaving it over until we have an opportunity of conferences with the other dominions. Secondly, if he feels that that should not be done,-I am not sure that he will not feel that-I suggest that this bill be referred to a special committee until we can see whether it is possible in the time at our disposal to go over the various sections and give them reasonable attention, paying particular attention to the seventy-five new sections which will require considerable work having regard to all the other duties which hon. members of this committee and of this house have to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth made two suggestions: First, that another conference should take place between the different parts of the empire in order to have uniformity of legislation. That conference has already taken place.

No. I have a copy of the conference of 1929 and of the agreement of 1931, but that was as regards the principles of the legislation. But I am talking about a committee on the legislation itself in order to draft a uniform act embodying those principles.

Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The different parts of the empire which were represented at that conference did not suggest anything of that kind. Moreover, they all agreed that they would enact legislation along the lines set out in the agreement. These are the words of the agreement:
His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland', Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, New Zealand, the Union of South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland, having considered the report of the conference on the operation of Dominion legislation and merchant shipping legislation, 1929, undertake to propose any necessary legislation and take such other steps as may be required for the purpose of giving full effect to the provisions of the present agreement with regard to merchant shipping.
So we are putting before parliament legislation that we have undertaken to enact along the lines suggested by this conference in order to preserve for some time to come uniformity in shipping laws within the empire.

Does my right hon. friend not know from his conversation and reports he has had there was a discussion about having a committee on commonwealth shipping legislation with regard to both admiralty courts and merchant shipping, that is another conference? Does he say he has not heard of that and it has not been suggested? It is not in the report but that is the way, as I understand it, in which the legislation would be adopted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I have not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I never heard of that. The agreement is very precise; we undertook to enact legislation along those lines.
Does the minister mean to say that the Dominion of Newfoundland has enacted legislation similar to this?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I never suggested that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not a dominion. There were other reasons besides that.

The Prime Minister should not rub that in to me-who, as he knows, was born there,-and the people of that island. Does the minister say that Newfoundland, whether it be a dominion or colony or whatever it may be, has adopted this legislation as it is in this book?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I never made that statement.
The minister tried to infer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: All I said was that the different parts of the empire, including Newfoundland, undertook to pass legislation along the lines of that which we have before us to-day.

Does my hon. friend want to have this legislation uniform with that of other parts of the empire? What I am saying is that he made use of the fact that Newfoundland had passed certain legislation. I know Newfoundland has not passed any such legislation as the minister is asking us to pass here to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have never said that Newfoundland had adopted such legislation as this. I have only stated that she is a party along with every other part of the empire to the agreement of 1931 to pass legislation along the lines mentioned in this agreement. It comprises almost the whole bill, not word for word or detail for detail, but the lines of the legislation.
Has the minister a copy of the Newfoundland legislation? Will he tell us whether it is the same as this or what difference there is? It is not like this at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The only thing I say is that we are putting before parliament legislation along the lines adopted by the conference in 1931.

But Newfoundland did not
adopt that; they passed legislation of their own which is not at all like this. Will my hon. friend) deny that or affirm it?
I would ask the hon. gentleman to address the Chair.
I was addressing the Chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Newfoundland is no longer a dominion.

The Minister of Marine tried to infer that Newfoundland had passed legislation similar to this. Before we go any further I would ask the Minister of Marine to bring before parliament the legislation which Newfoundland passed since the conference spoken of by the Prime Minister, who tried to make out that because Alexander Johnston and Lucien Pacaud, who know nothing about ships or marine matters, signed certain agreements in London, the sailors of this country should stand behind this legislation and have it put through parliament. That is not right. The Newfoundland government had more sense
Canada Shipping Act

than to pass any stupid, foolish legislation such as we are being asked to pass to-night and which has been brought down from another part of this parliament.

Might I ask the minister whether the conference of 1931 which I understand was international, embodied anything that would bind this country to make uniform legislation in so far as coastal navigation within the Dominion of Canada is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No.
I understand the minister to say no. Then so far as our coastal regulations are concerned, that is a matter of our own?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Surely.

It is in regard to that I am raising the objection. If our coastal regulations and those governing our fishing fleet are embodied in this legislation, let the minister have passed those clauses that come under the jurisdiction, if you like, of the conference of 1931, but in the name of conscience let him give us a chance to consult our constituents in regard to coastal and fishing regulations, let him not impose them on us.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There are no fishing regulations in the bill.
There are.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I would like my hon. friend to point them out.

There are definitions as to what a fishing vessel is; there are definitions and clauses defining what a fishing vessel has to do, how she shall register, who shall sail her, who shall be in command, what the sailors shall do. This is right in the bill; the minister cannot deny it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is mistaken.
I am not mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As to the fishermen, the same law as heretofore is in this bill. I listened to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough a minute ago state that the fishing boats wore bound to have certificated masters.
Quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is nothing of the kind in the bill. If my hon. friend will read clause 113 he will see that ships solely employed in fishing are exempted from having certificated masters or mates.
Does the minister mean to tell me that he can find any one vessel called a fishing vessel that is solely engaged in the fishing business?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Why not?

Surely the minister does not wish to leave that impression with the committee. They have their fishing seasons and at other times they are employed at something else. If they are employed at anything else; if they are employed in taking supplies to far off fishing districts and are not engaged on a fishing trip, they come under this legislation. Especially do they come under it if they have an auxiliary attached of over three horsepower; then they have to have a captain with a certificate. More than that, they have to have an engineer.
A certificated engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is mistaken.

I am not mistaken, and I
do not care where the minister gets his information. This is in the bill, and I know what its application means.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That does not apply
to those small boats.

Let me give the minister an example. The W. S. Loggie concern at Chatham, New Brunswick, one of the largest fishing concerns in the maritime provinces, own a large number of vessels. They have vessels engaged in fishing and at other times the same boats are engaged in transporting their fish coastwise from one factory to another or to headquarters. Those vessels have auxiliaries. Under this legislation no captain of such a vessel can operate it unless he has a captain's certificate. Let me give another instance. Take the fishermen of Miscou Harbour, using vessels of ten to twenty tons. I think the largest about twenty-five. They fish all season; they will fish during the herring season in the spring and in the fall herring season, and after the fall fishing season they are recognized as freight boats; they transport their product to the markets at Chatham, Newcastle, Bathurst and Campbellton-coastal traffic. They have auxiliaries; they would come under this bill, and the captains will have to have a master's certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The same as the
present law.
No, it is not.

It is not.

Canada Shipping Act

Get the old act and read it. If it is the same law as before, two hundred and seventy-five Sail in the fishing fleet in the northern section of New Brunswick, the county I represent, are violating the law every day. I know it is not so; there is no use trying to put the like of that over on us, because we have experience.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) has suggested that one of three courses might be taken in respect to this legislation. The accuracy of his recital of the historic facts I think no one will question. But we have proceeded with this legislation not idly, just to do something, but because we recognized that there was an obligation upon us with respect to it. We are a maritime community with shores on the Pacific and the Atlantic. When this matter was agreed to in 1931 we prepared a bill, and because of the fact that there are many difficulties involved and we were endeavouring to secure some measure of uniformity with respect to the principles -not,the details-I had the draft bill sent to and subsequently discussed it with the officials who are responsible in Great Britain for legislation of this character. Many suggestions were made; some of them we could easily accept, some we could not. Australia has not yet enacted the legislation. I think it is not unfair to say that they expect us to proceed first, because they have coastal difficulties to meet and we have coastal difficulties to meet; but we have in common with them the general principles to be accepted dealing with shipping legislation. Now, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot) has very properly pointed out that with respect to coastal matters there is of course no uniformity. With respect to small details as to the size of ships that require certificated masters there is no suggestion about uniformity being necessary; it is not even hinted. But with respect to the large principles that govern the whole shipping business, obviously the largest shipping country in the world being Great Britain, we are anxious to obtain the benefit of their wide experience. If I say to this committee that I had the privilege of discussing it with those who are regarded as the foremost authorities in the world I but state the simple fact. The solicitors who are responsible for the advice to the various departments in Great Britain that have to deal with this matter were good enough to give us the benefit of their judgment; that advice was in the hands of the minister, and when the minister had the act redrafted we had the benefit of all 74726-249
their experience placed at our disposal in the form of a memorandum that would enable us to proceed in the best possible manner. If, as the bon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough has suggested, this bill is but the product of the paste pot and scissors, obviously the enactment of it is a simple matter. If on the other hand it is a combination of old and new provisions, as it is, this committee will study carefully the terms expressing the meaning of parliament in the light of the existing legislation both in the Merchant Shipping Act and the Canada Shipping Act that we have had for years. It has been suggested that that can better be done by a special committee than in committee of the whole. The practice in England is to take it after second reading in committee of the whole. We have departed from that practice because sometimes we become very garrulous in committees of the whole and have failed to direct our attention to the particular sections under consideration. In Great Britain it is the practice to go into committee of the whole in respect to measures that are government measures, such for instance as the Home Rule bill, local rate bills and matters of that kind. We have recently departed from that practice. In the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when parliament had to deal with the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk, it did not send the matter to a special committee but went into committee of the whole house. Delegations do not appear at the bar of the house to represent their views; the government of the day assumes responsibility. That was the practice in this house, but conditions changed and it was thought that to refer a bill to a special committee was the easiest way to get rid of some responsibility.
It was not done to get rid of responsibility.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not suggesting that was the hon. gentleman's intention.
That was not the intention of anyone.
It was to deal with technical matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For technical matters the government must assume responsibility.

I think the Prime Minister conveyed a wrong impression when he suggested that bills were referred to a special committee to escape responsibility. I do not think that was the intention of the government. I think it was because it was considered a better way to deal with them.

Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One of the best instances is the Georgian Bay canal bill.
Well, take the Bank Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The government of the day attempted to evade responsibility by giving the Georgian Bay canal bill second reading to save its face and sending it to the committee for the purpose of seeing it killed, one man voting for it. That is not the practice in the British parliament. In connection with the Bank Act I pointed out the other day that the practice had grown up of dealing with such bills in the manner followed this session. But with respect to this legislation there is no necessity for sending it to any committee. The government of the day assumes the responsibility for the bill. If tonight we had spent the time in passing sections that have been on the statute books of this country for many years we would perhaps have come to the sections to which the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) has referred, although he had no right to refer to them in committee of the whole until they were reached; and then the arguments he has made and the arguments which the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough may make may be sufficiently powerful to induce the government to accept their view, and accept it gladly.
Then there is this further point: one must face actualities at some time or other. We have had this bill now considered for three years, two years in form, one year in the nebulous condition of general principles that were to be observed. We have printed and circulated it one session, then rewritten it, reorganized it in the light of views and criticisms received, and the fact that it has been considered in another place is only some evidence that in its present form it has received the best consideration that the men who were charged with responsibility of dealing with it in committee could give to it. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth says, that that is no reason why we should shirk our duty with respect to it. I have never asserted that we should. But there is nothing in the bill that should give this house any difficulty if it will apply itself to the consideration of it in the light of the existing legislation and remember that the new sections are not numerous but are important because they confer upon Canada jurisdiction in matters about which some difficulties might have arisen in times past. We wish this to be upon the statute books. If we are ever going to get shipping bills within the other members

of the commonwealth it is desirable that this country should take the lead, not for that purpose but because they look to us to do so, and they know that we have had the benefit of the best assistance that could be given to us in Great Britain. We are merely endeavouring to carry out not a compulsory obligation but an undertaking. The minister has just read from the document which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth has in his hand, a statement of what our obligations were in 1931. It is not a compulsory undertaking that all the dominions would do so; we undertook to do something. Now we have done it. At [DOT] the end of this bill we have provided that it shall not come into force until proclamation. That is, once enacted as a statute it then becomes something upon which attention may be focused and as to which constructive amendments may be suggested. That section also provides that even the whole of the bill need not be brought into force on proclamation, that parts of it may be proclaimed if so desired. That is section 719, which reads:
This act shall not come into force until a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette: provided that he may, in the same manner and from time to time, bring any portion or portions only of this act into force.
I need hardly remind the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth that this is done to meet the very condition to which I have referred. Conditions in various parts of the commonwealth are not the same, but with respect to the large principles of the measure, when we have enacted our measure we proclaim, we will say, one hundred sections that deal with one particular phase. That has met with general approval, and that is the end of it. Later we proclaim another hundred sections, because they have been approved by the various sections of the commonwealth. Finally we may proclaim the remainder. This section is drawn in this way in an endeavour to ensure that effect shall be given to the undertaking which, while as I say it was not compulsory in its character, involved the idea that we would proceed with some degree of reasonable promptitude to give effect to the promise which was made, namely that we would introduce legislation with respect to shipping on certain principles.
There is one other phase of it which is rather important. The schedules or annexes to this legislation, which cover nearly two hundred pages, represent conventions concluded at Geneva, at London and at other places. They are not conventions which we can disregard. Not only did we sign them;

Canada Shipping Act
we ratified them. Not only were they ratified by executive action; in the main they have been submitted to and approved by this house.
Is there anything more needed in that respect?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned that, because if he will take the trouble to look through the bill he will find that the relation of the shipping act itself to the terms and provisions of the various conventions becomes of considerable importance. There are several sections here; I will not take time to turn them up. We find the words, "subject to the provisions of the load line convention," "subject to the convention dealing with labour matters," using the word in the broad sense, because otherwise you can hardly use it in regard to seamen who are under articles, and so on. Broadly speaking, the provisions of the conventions must be considered. Then you have the questions of signals, rules of navigation, radio communication and matters of that kind. These are covered by conventions, and they are woven into the statute. In large part those are the new sections, because needless to say when the first act was written there was no such thing as radio or communication between sea and shore as we know it. Fog signals were not of the character we now have, and in fact the rules of the road have been changed. The load line convention is related also to the provisions of the statute.
And the salvage of airships.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman; that was the other matter to which my attention was being directed. Following the loss of the Titanic there was a convention dealing with questions of life boats, rafts, life jackets, life buoys and so on. All these matters, while the subjects of conventions, by this statute are woven into the texture of the law, which the committee will observe is altogether different from merely having a convention which baldly declares what we are to do, without weaving it into the statute itself.
It is for these reasons that this provision is inserted in the statute which contemplates that the statute may come into force on proclamation, not necessarily as a whole but one part and then another part, in order that there may be no inconvenience caused to anyone.
May I remind this committee that there are some matters dealt with in this statute that relate to these conventions, and the 74728-2495
interrelation between the terms of the conventions and the statute is such that we cannot, without violating our international undertakings. do otherwise than pass the statute in the terms in which it appears. A moment ago the hon. member for Gloucester said something that greatly impressed me. He said, "If this be so, a large number of people are violating the law," presumably without knowing it. As a matter of fact there has been going on in this country continuously, without knowledge, because of changes that have been made in some of these matters, a disregard of the statute, and I think everyone realizes that substantial effort has been made last year and again this year to try to bring to the attention of as many people as possible the fact that we have assumed international obligations. The ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has been president of the League of Nations Society in Canada. The League of Nations is the organization that promoted these conventions. A moment ago the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) made some reference to matters touching the lives of seamen, their articles, their clothing, their food, their care when ill in marine hospitals, the disposition of their property if they died, and so on. All these matters were dealt with in days gone by in Great Britain by the Board of Trade, and the regulations of that body. In these conventions that we have made we have dealt with these very things, and the statute merely endeavours to relate the convention to the enactments of parliament, which of course is of first importance.
Does anyone suggest for a single moment that anyone sitting on this side of the house, with ministerial responsibility, is anxious to undertake unnecessary labour? Does anyone suggest that most of us have not enough to do? We have a duty to discharge: we may not discharge it to the entire satisfaction of hon. gentlemen opposite, but we will have to do the best we can. If I had not believed there was an obligation resting upon us to deal with this legislation I would not have introduced it. It will be recalled that reference was made to this legislation in the speech from the throne. The question of introducing it in this house rather than in another place became important in view of the fact that at this session this house undertook the responsibility with respect to the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act, and a committee was sitting that was dealing with matters of great public importance. Under those circumstances we concluded that in another house this bill could best receive, in the first instance, that attention which its
Canada Shipping Act

importance demanded. While the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was quite correct in saying that a stenographic report of what took place was not kept, nevertheless during the holidays and over the week-ends selected small subcommittees continued to sit and to deal with every phase of the bill. Draftsmen endeavoured to reconcile the various statutes which had heretofore existed with those which it was desired to enact. Suggestions made by those who had to deal with these matters were considered, and the fact is that in recent times no legislation which has been submitted to either house of parliament has received more consideration than this received in another place. I am not for one single moment endeavouring to assert that because that has been done we are relieved of our responsibility, but I do say that with respect to legislation of this kind these houses of parliament have co-equal jurisdiction, and it is idle to suggest that one house rather than another should receive all the measures of an administration. In fact, I believe as days go by it will be found that the other branch of parliament can be more effectively used than it has been. That is my conviction with respect to it. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The idea of referring
this bill to a committee I must, with all deference, disregard at the moment. I suggest that to-morrow, after we have dealt with the resolution on the Franchise Act, we should proceed with this bill and continue to proceed with it on Thursday, on Friday, on Monday and until such time as we have made the necessary progress to enable us to deal with those sections about which there is great controversy.
When there is great controversy and difference of opinion with regard to certain sections, while this government must assume the responsibility for the legislation, I promise this chamber that any reasonable suggestions which are put forward will receive not only every consideration, but if in the view of some bon. members of wide experience in this chamber, it is thought that we should change, modify, amend or deal with a section in any way, we will try to the best of our ability to accommodate ourselves to such view. That is so, because in domestic matters no principle concerns us except the well being of the people as a whole, our own people. I think the hon. member for Shelbume-Yar-mouth and myself are at one as to that, that the broad principles embodied in the agree-

ment of 1931 did not deal with our domestic situation at all, our inland lakes, our inland waters or, for instance, lake Winnipeg, the Red river, the Saskatchewan river, or those major rivers and lakes which constitute the great watershed, including lakes Superior and Michigan and the others. But when we deal with what may be called sea-going responsibilities, on the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, we are endeavouring to enact legislation which is prepared to conform to the provisions of international conventions to which we became a party. Whether we acted wisely or not I cannot say, but the late administration as well as the present one must accept the responsibility.
That is all I can usefully say as to the purpose behind and the reasons governing us, and the earnestness of our desire to place legislation upon the statute book not simply to have more work or to supply a gorge of legislation, but rather to do that which we conceive to be our duty to our own people consonant with the obligations of an international character which we have assumed as signatories to various conventions on maritime questions, as well as the obligations which we assumed ip 1931.

I cannot speak with the
same authority as has the Prime Minister with regard to the international obligations to which he has referred, but I would take it as this House of Commons has approved of, for instance, the load lines convention and these other conventions that it is possible by regulation to put them into force, and thus carry out any convention obligations which we had. I do not think it is absolutely necessary to pass this legislation in order to make effective those conventions practically all of which have already been accepted by this House of Commons and are I think already in force. That is my first observation, affecting international obligations.
With regard to coastal and inland waters, if I understand my right hon. friend correctly the law outlined in the new bill is practically the same as in the old. If that is so it seems to me the statute as it is to-day is sufficient; and there is no necessity for passing any legislation in that respect.
That leaves only that which my right hon. friend termed sea-going responsibilities, affecting deep sea navigation, our responsibilities on the high seas and with regard to seamen, safety of life, and so on. It seems to me those factors fit in with and are part of the agreement to which he has referred and to which the Minister of Marine has referred. I have read that agreement, and it seems to me

Questions
that before legislation is actually brought down consultation is contemplated between the various commonwealths. I find that article 16 in part VI of the British Commonwealth Merchant Shipping Agreement provides:
The standards of qualification to be required of applicants for certificates of competency and of service shall so far as possible be equal and alike throughout the British commonwealth, and shall not be lower than those at present established.
How can we have uniformity and have them equal and alike unless we have consultation among the different dominions concerned to ascertain what those standards should be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: After the statute is passed.

No; that would mean that the only way we could have uniformity is by others passing some kind of statute, and we would have to make our statute uniform with theirs. That is not what this agreement contemplates, neither does it mean that we take the lead and set up a standard for them to follow. I am just trying to point the argument I tried to make, namely that the agreement of 1931 contemplated consultation before our statute was passed. Then, respecting offences on board ship I find in part IX, article 23, of the agreement the following:
Reciprocal arrangements shall be made for conferring jurisdiction on the lines of section 686 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894, with respect to offences committed on board ships registered in any part of the commonwealth.
How can we make reciprocal arrangements without having previous consultation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You have to have your
statute first.

I submit not. You have a conference, and pass the statute afterwards. Then, turning to part II, standards of safety, I find the following as article 6:
While each part of the commonwealth will from time to time determine the standards with which its ships shall be required to comply in all matters relating to safety, every endeavour will be made to preserve uniformity and to maintain the standards at present in force.
You cannot do that without consultation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Since then we have an
international provision ratified by this house.
If we have an international provision already ratified we do not need the statute at all.
It is not international. Every British dominion has its own law.

I suggest this, that notwithstanding what they do in the British House of Commons, we have been dealing through committees with matters such as the one now before us. We dealt with the Bank Act through a committee, and we did the same with the central bank act. My right hon. friend, regardless of constitutional practice, will agree that that is the most efficient parliamentary method of dealing with it. There would be more real progress made if the matter were referred to a committee which could give it intensive study not merely from three o'clock to eleven o'clock, but could sit in the mornings and, if necessary, establish subcommittees.
I am disappointed that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to accept the suggestion, but I have made it in the spirit in which he replied, namely that we are both anxious to get on with the work of the house. I do feel that he defeats that object when at this late date- or, what is supposed to be a late date in the session-he places this voluminous bill on the table of the house and compels us to pass it through committee of the whole.
Progress reported.
